modules.title: Foundations: Data Structures, Algorithms and Arrays

topics.title: Data Structures: Basic Terminologies
topics.definition: A data structure is a way of arranging data in memory so that it can be used quickly and neatly.

children.title: Data item and field
children.definition: A single value is a data item; a field is one named place that stores a value inside a record.

children.title: Record and file
children.definition: A record groups related items about one entity; a file is a collection of similar records.

children.title: Primitive and non-primitive structures
children.definition: Primitive structures hold single values such as int or char, while non-primitive structures are built from them, such as arrays and lists.

children.title: Linear and non-linear structures
children.definition: Linear structures arrange elements in a sequence, while non-linear structures such as trees and graphs arrange them in levels or networks.

children.title: Static and dynamic structures
children.definition: Static structures have a fixed size decided at compile time; dynamic structures grow and shrink at run time.

children.title: Operations on data structures
children.definition: Insertion, deletion, traversal, searching, sorting and merging are the standard operations performed on any structure.

card.explanation: Every program keeps data somewhere, and how you keep it decides how fast you can work with it. A data structure is just that arrangement plus the rules for adding, finding and removing items. Two words appear everywhere: data item (one single value) and record (a group of related values kept together). When people say a structure is efficient, they mean the operations you need most often take less time or less memory.
card.example: Think of your college bag. Books stacked flat are easy to add on top but slow to search. Books in labelled pockets are slower to fill but you can grab the right one instantly. Same books, different arrangement, different speed.

quiz.q: What does a data structure mainly decide?
options: How many users can open the program
The license of the programming language
How data is arranged in memory and which operations are fast
The colour scheme of a program
quiz.why: A data structure is the arrangement plus the rules for inserting, searching and deleting.

quiz.q: A single value such as the age 21 is called a:
options: Data item
Structure
Field group
Record
quiz.why: A single value is a data item; a group of related values stored together is a record.

quiz.q: Which statement about data structure terms is NOT correct?
options: A record is a group of related values kept together
A structure is only for storing data, never for finding it
Efficiency means the operations you use most are fast
A data item is one single value kept on its own
quiz.why: A data structure is the arrangement plus the rules for adding, finding and removing items, so finding data is part of its job.

quiz.q: A team keeps student marks in a plain list and finds one student by checking from the top every time. According to the card, what is the real problem?
options: The marks are grouped as records instead of data items
The list holds more data items than memory allows
The language they use has no built-in array type
The arrangement makes their most used operation slow
quiz.why: The same data arranged differently would make the operation they repeat most take less time, and that choice is the data structure.

card.examTip: Define data structure first, then give one line each on data item and record - one mark is usually kept for the terminology.

topics.title: Algorithms: Definition
topics.definition: An algorithm is a finite step-by-step list of instructions that turns given input into the required output.

children.title: Finiteness
children.definition: The algorithm must end after a limited number of steps.

children.title: Definiteness
children.definition: Every step must be unambiguous and precisely stated.

children.title: Input and output
children.definition: Zero or more inputs are supplied and at least one output is produced.

children.title: Effectiveness
children.definition: Each step must be basic enough to be carried out in finite time.

card.explanation: An algorithm must finish after a limited number of steps, so it is finite and not an endless loop. Every step must be clear enough that anyone can follow it without guessing (that is called being unambiguous). It should take zero or more inputs and must produce at least one output. The same algorithm can be written in any language - the logic stays the same, only the spelling changes.
card.example: A recipe for making tea is an algorithm: take water, boil, add tea powder, add milk, boil again, serve. Inputs are water and powder, output is tea, and each step is clear.

quiz.q: Which property means an algorithm must stop after a limited number of steps?
options: Finiteness
Redundancy
Modularity
Ambiguity
quiz.why: Finiteness means the steps are limited, so execution always ends.

quiz.q: Minimum number of outputs an algorithm must produce:
options: One
Two
As many as its inputs
Zero
quiz.why: An algorithm must produce at least one output, otherwise the work is pointless.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a property that an algorithm must have?
options: Brevity, so it is written in the fewest possible lines
Finiteness, so it stops after a limited number of steps
Definiteness, so every step is clear and unambiguous
Effectiveness, so each step is simple enough to carry out
quiz.why: There is no brevity property; an algorithm may be long as long as it is finite, definite, effective and produces output.

quiz.q: A friend writes steps to find the largest of three numbers, but one step says only 'compare them properly'. Which property does that step break?
options: Input, because the numbers are already given
Effectiveness, because the answer must be printed
Definiteness, because the step is not unambiguous
Finiteness, because the steps must come to an end
quiz.why: Every step has to be clear enough to follow without guessing, and 'compare them properly' leaves the reader guessing.

card.examTip: Write the definition and then list five properties: finiteness, definiteness, input, output, effectiveness.

topics.title: Algorithms: Pseudocode Representation
topics.definition: Pseudocode is a rough, language-free way of writing an algorithm using plain words and simple keywords.

children.title: Keywords used in pseudocode
children.definition: READ, PRINT, IF-ELSE, WHILE, FOR, REPEAT and RETURN express control flow in plain words.

children.title: Rules for writing pseudocode
children.definition: One statement per line, indentation for nesting and no dependence on the syntax of any language.

children.title: Algorithm versus flowchart versus program
children.definition: A flowchart uses symbols, pseudocode uses words and a program uses a real language - all three describe the same logic.

card.explanation: Pseudocode keeps the logic but drops the strict grammar of a real language, so you can focus on the steps. Common keywords are READ, PRINT, IF-ELSE, WHILE, FOR and RETURN. It cannot be run on a computer directly - it is a plan that you convert into C++ or Java later. Writing pseudocode first makes the coding stage short because the thinking is already done.
card.example: A pseudocode for finding the biggest number: READ a, b; IF a > b THEN PRINT a ELSE PRINT b. That is the whole logic before any coding.

quiz.q: Pseudocode differs from a real program because it:
options: Runs faster than compiled code
Follows no strict grammar and cannot be executed directly
Needs a compiler
Works only in Java
quiz.why: Pseudocode is a loose, human-readable plan that is not executable.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a typical pseudocode keyword?
options: WHILE
PRINT
import java.util
READ
quiz.why: Import statements belong to a real language; pseudocode stays language-free.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT something pseudocode does?
options: Runs on the computer without being translated first
Shortens the coding stage because the thinking is done
Keeps the algorithm's logic in plain readable words
Uses simple keywords such as READ, WHILE and PRINT
quiz.why: Pseudocode cannot be executed directly; it is a plan that you translate into a language such as C++ or Java later.

quiz.q: You must show the logic of a payroll program to a teacher who does not know Java. What should you hand over?
options: The complete Java source with comments added
Only the final printed output of the program
A list of the input files the program reads
Pseudocode using plain steps and simple keywords
quiz.why: Pseudocode keeps the logic and drops the strict grammar, so a reader who does not know Java can still check the steps.

card.examTip: If a question says 'write an algorithm', pseudocode or numbered steps are both accepted - pick one style and stay consistent.

topics.title: Time Complexity
topics.definition: Time complexity counts how the running time of an algorithm grows when the input size grows.

children.title: Basic operation count
children.definition: Count the operation that dominates, such as comparisons in a search or multiplications in a matrix product.

children.title: Growth rate
children.definition: The way the operation count increases as n increases: constant, logarithmic, linear, quadratic or exponential.

children.title: Asymptotic analysis for large n
children.definition: Constants and lower order terms are ignored because only the trend for large inputs matters.

card.explanation: It is not the stopwatch time in seconds, because that changes with every machine. Instead we count the basic operations and express them as a function of input size n. This tells you what happens when the data becomes large - doubling the input may double the work, or square it. A smaller growth rate is always preferred, because it survives big inputs better.
card.example: Searching a shelf of 100 files one by one takes about 100 checks; with 1000 files it takes about 1000 checks. The work doubles when files grow ten times, so the growth is linear.

quiz.q: Time complexity mainly measures:
options: Exact seconds on your laptop
Growth of operations as input size grows
Number of lines in the program
Memory used by the compiler
quiz.why: It is a growth measure as a function of input size, not wall-clock seconds.

quiz.q: If the input size doubles and the work also doubles, the growth is:
options: Constant
Linear
Quadratic
Logarithmic
quiz.why: Work proportional to n means linear growth, written O(n).

quiz.q: Which statement about time complexity is NOT correct?
options: It is the stopwatch time measured on the lab computer
It shows how the work grows as the data becomes large
A smaller growth rate survives a large input better
It counts basic operations as a function of input size
quiz.why: Stopwatch time changes with every machine; time complexity counts operations against n so the comparison is portable.

quiz.q: Your teacher raises the test data from 1,000 to 10,000 records and the running time grows about a hundred times. What does that show?
options: The work grows in a straight line with the input
The work stays the same for every input size
The work grows more slowly than the input
The work grows with the square of the input size
quiz.why: Ten times the input producing a hundred times the work is the n squared pattern, not a linear one.

quiz.q: An algorithm always performs 4n + 20 basic operations. About how many operations does it perform for n = 100?
options: About 120
About 4,020
About 10,400
About 420
quiz.why: 4 x 100 + 20 = 420; the growth is written O(n), but the actual count still uses the real expression.

card.examTip: Never write 'time complexity = 5 seconds' in the exam; always express it as a function of n.

topics.title: Space Complexity
topics.definition: Space complexity is the total memory an algorithm needs, counting both the fixed part and the extra working space.

children.title: Fixed part
children.definition: Memory for the program code, constants and simple variables that does not depend on the input size.

children.title: Variable part
children.definition: Memory for the data structures whose size depends on the input, such as arrays or recursion frames.

children.title: Auxiliary space
children.definition: Extra working memory used beyond the input itself, which is what "in-place" algorithms try to minimise.

card.explanation: The fixed part holds code, constants and simple variables, and it never changes with input size. The variable part grows with the input, for example the array that stores n values or the extra array created during sorting. When we compare algorithms we usually talk about the extra space beyond the input, called auxiliary space. An algorithm that uses a constant amount of extra space is called in-place.
card.example: Merging two sorted lists into a new list needs a second list of the same size - that extra space is the cost. Swapping two numbers needs only one small temporary variable, so it is in-place.

quiz.q: Auxiliary space means:
options: Memory for the input itself
Extra working memory used besides the input
Memory of the operating system
Disk space of the program file
quiz.why: Auxiliary space is the extra memory used over and above the given input.

quiz.q: An algorithm that uses only a fixed amount of extra memory is called:
options: In-place
Dynamic
Static
Recursive
quiz.why: In-place algorithms need O(1) extra space.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT counted as auxiliary space?
options: The memory holding the input array itself
A temporary array created while sorting the input
A second list built while merging two sorted lists
One small variable used to swap two values
quiz.why: Auxiliary space is the extra working memory beyond the input, so the input array is not part of it.

quiz.q: You must merge two sorted lists of 500 names each into a new list without touching the originals. What is the extra memory cost?
options: A second list of about 1,000 names, O(n) auxiliary
One temporary variable only, so O(1) auxiliary
No extra memory, because both lists are sorted
About half a list, so O(n/2) auxiliary space
quiz.why: Building a new merged list needs a second list as large as the total input, which is O(n) auxiliary space.

quiz.q: An algorithm uses exactly three extra variables whatever the input size. How is its auxiliary space written?
options: O(1), a constant amount of extra memory
O(n), because extra memory grows with input
O(3n), because it keeps three variables
O(log n), because the variables are small
quiz.why: A fixed three variables never grow with n, so the auxiliary space is constant, O(1), which makes the algorithm in-place.

card.examTip: Mention both time and space complexity for every algorithm you describe; marks are often split between them.

topics.title: Efficiency of Algorithms (Best, Average, Worst Case)
topics.definition: An algorithm is efficient when it solves the problem using the least time and memory, and we judge that using three cases: best, average and worst.

children.title: Best case
children.definition: The input arrangement for which the algorithm finishes fastest, such as finding the target at the first position.

children.title: Average case
children.definition: The expected cost over typical inputs, often calculated with probability assumptions.

children.title: Worst case
children.definition: The input arrangement that forces the maximum work; it is the guarantee reported in most analyses.

children.title: Why the worst case is reported
children.definition: It gives an upper limit that holds for every input, so it is the safest measure of performance.

card.explanation: The best case is the luckiest input, the worst case is the unluckiest input and the average case is the typical input. Worst case is the one usually reported, because it is the guarantee you can depend on. Comparing two algorithms means comparing their growth rates, not their code length. A shorter program can easily be the slower one.
card.example: Linear search on a list of names: you find the name first try (best), find it in the middle (average) or scan the whole list (worst). The worst case is what you promise the user.

quiz.q: Which case do we normally report for an algorithm?
options: Worst case
Any one case
Best case
Average case
quiz.why: Worst case gives the upper guarantee, so it is the standard choice.

quiz.q: Best case of linear search when the target is the first element:
options: O(log n)
O(n)
quiz.why: One comparison is enough, so it is constant time.

quiz.q: Which statement about the three cases is NOT correct?
options: Comparing algorithms means comparing code length
Best case is the luckiest input and worst the unluckiest
Worst case is reported because it is a guarantee
Average case is the typical input seen in practice
quiz.why: Algorithms are compared by growth rate, not by how short the code is; a shorter program can easily be the slower one.

quiz.q: Two programs solve the same problem. One is 40 lines and the other is 200 lines. How should you compare them?
options: By line count, because shorter code is always faster
By the best case only, because that is the target
By which language they happen to be written in
By their growth rates, not by their line counts
quiz.why: The card states that comparing algorithms means comparing growth rates, and code length says nothing about how the work grows.

quiz.q: A search on 1,000 items takes 1 comparison in the best case, about 500 on average and 1,000 in the worst case. What growth does the average case show?
options: Linear growth, because the work rises with the input
Constant growth, because the average never changes
Quadratic growth, because the input is squared
Logarithmic growth, because it halves each step
quiz.why: About n/2 comparisons is still a straight-line rise with n, so the average case of linear search is O(n).

card.examTip: For every search or sort question, state best, average and worst complexity in one line each.

topics.title: Big-O (O) Notation
topics.definition: Big-O notation, read as 'order of', gives the upper limit of an algorithm's growth - the most work it will ever do for a large input.

children.title: Definition of the upper bound
children.definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than g times some constant for all sufficiently large n.

children.title: Dropping constants and lower terms
children.definition: 3n squared + 5n + 9 becomes O(n squared), because the highest order term decides the trend.

children.title: Common growth rates in increasing order
children.definition: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n squared) < O(2 to the n).

card.explanation: Big-O ignores small details like constants and lower terms, because they stop mattering for large inputs. So 3n + 5 becomes simply O(n), and n squared + 100n becomes O(n squared). O stands for the ceiling: the running time will not grow faster than this. That is why O(1) beats O(log n), which beats O(n), which beats O(n squared).
card.example: If a program prints every student name once, it does about n steps. Whether the class has 60 or 600 students, the pattern is the same, so we simply say O(n).

quiz.q: Simplify 5n + 20 to Big-O:
options: O(5n)
O(n)
quiz.why: Constants are dropped in Big-O, so 5n + 20 is O(n).

quiz.q: Big-O notation describes:
options: Upper bound
Average memory
Lower bound
Exact bound only
quiz.why: Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound on growth.

quiz.q: Which statement about Big-O notation is NOT correct?
options: It keeps the smaller terms, so n squared + 100n stays as it is
O(1) is better than O(n), which is better than O(n squared)
It gives the upper limit of growth for a large input
It drops constants, so 3n + 5 becomes O(n)
quiz.why: Smaller terms are dropped as well, so n squared + 100n simplifies to O(n squared) because the squared term dominates.

quiz.q: Your program does 3n + 5 operations and your friend writes it as O(3n + 5). What should you write instead?
options: O(5), because 5 is the smallest part of it
O(n squared), because terms are multiplied
O(n), because constants and lower terms are dropped
O(3n), because the constant 3 has to stay
quiz.why: Big-O keeps only the fastest growing term with its constant removed, so 3n + 5 simplifies to O(n).

quiz.q: For a very large input, which of these orders needs the fewest operations?
options: O(log n)
O(n squared)
O(n)
quiz.why: Constant time does not grow at all, so O(1) beats O(log n), which beats O(n), which beats O(n squared).

card.examTip: Practise simplifying expressions fast - dropping constants is worth easy marks in the first question itself.

topics.title: Omega and Theta Notations
topics.definition: Omega notation gives the lower limit (the least work) and Theta notation gives a tight limit where the upper and lower growth match.

children.title: Omega notation (lower bound)
children.definition: f(n) = Omega(g(n)) means f grows at least as fast as g, so g is the floor of the growth.

children.title: Theta notation (tight bound)
children.definition: f(n) = Theta(g(n)) means f is bounded both above and below by g, so the growth rate is exact.

children.title: Roof, floor and room
children.definition: Big-O is the roof, Omega is the floor and Theta is a room of exactly that size.

card.explanation: Omega, written as the Greek letter, says the running time will not grow slower than a certain function - it is the floor. Theta is used when the best and worst growth rates are of the same order, so it pins the function from both sides. In short, Big-O is the roof, Omega is the floor and Theta is a room of the same size. A function can have many upper bounds but only one tight Theta bound for a given order.
card.example: For an algorithm that always does n comparisons whatever the input, you can safely say Theta(n), because the floor and roof are both n.

quiz.q: Which notation gives a lower bound on growth?
options: None of these
Big-O
Omega
Theta
quiz.why: Omega is the asymptotic lower bound, the floor of the growth.

quiz.q: Theta notation is used when:
options: The input is small
Recursion is used
Only the worst case is known
Upper and lower bounds have the same order
quiz.why: Theta needs matching upper and lower bounds, so it is a tight bound.

quiz.q: Which statement about the three notations is NOT correct?
options: Big-O is the floor and Omega is the roof of growth
A function can have many upper bounds but one tight Theta
Omega gives the least work an algorithm can do
Theta is used when the two bounds have the same order
quiz.why: It is the other way round: Big-O is the roof (upper bound) and Omega is the floor (lower bound).

quiz.q: An algorithm performs exactly n comparisons for every input of size n. Which statement can you write?
options: O(n squared), because that is the safest bound
Theta(n), because the floor and the roof are both n
Only O(1), because the work per item is fixed
Only Omega(1), because the work never grows
quiz.why: When the lower and upper bounds have the same order, Theta pins the function from both sides: Theta(n).

quiz.q: An algorithm's work always lies between 2n and 5n. Which notation describes it exactly?
options: Theta(2n), because 2n is the lower bound
Theta(5n), because 5n is the upper bound
Theta(n squared), because 5n is more than n
Theta(n), because both bounds have the same order
quiz.why: Theta ignores the constants on both sides and keeps the order that both bounds share, which is n.

card.examTip: Draw the roof-floor-room picture in the margin; examiners love a diagram with O, Omega and Theta labelled.

topics.title: Arrays: One Dimensional and Multidimensional
topics.definition: An array is a fixed-size block of memory holding items of the same type, where each item is reached by its index number.

children.title: One dimensional array
children.definition: A single list of elements reached by one index, stored in consecutive memory locations.

children.title: Multidimensional array
children.definition: A table-like array with two or more indices, such as a matrix with rows and columns.

children.title: Address calculation in row major and column major order
children.definition: Row major stores a row at a time so address = base + (i * columns + j) * size; column major stores a column at a time.

children.title: Operations on arrays
children.definition: Traversal, insertion, deletion, searching and sorting, where insertion and deletion need shifting.

children.title: Advantages and limitations
children.definition: Constant time access by index is the advantage; fixed size and costly middle insertion are the limitations.

card.explanation: Because items sit next to each other in memory, the address of any item can be calculated directly, so reading arr[i] takes constant time. Indexing normally starts at 0, so the first item is arr[0] and the last is arr[n-1]. A one dimensional array is a simple list, while a two dimensional array is a table with rows and columns. The big limitation is that you must decide the size in advance, and inserting or deleting in the middle means shifting many items.
card.example: A class attendance register is a 1D array of names. A seating chart with rows and columns is a 2D array, where seat [3][2] means row 3, column 2.

quiz.q: Why is arr[i] a constant-time operation?
options: The array is sorted first
Address is computed directly from index and element size
The compiler searches the array
Arrays use hashing
quiz.why: Random access comes from the address formula base + i * size.

quiz.q: In a 1D array of size n, the last valid index is:
options: n
quiz.why: Indexing starts at 0, so the last index is n - 1.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a property of an array as described on the card?
options: The size grows and shrinks freely while the program runs
Inserting in the middle means shifting the later items
Items of the same type sit next to each other in memory
Any item is reached directly by its index number
quiz.why: An array is a fixed-size block, so its size is decided in advance and the shifting cost is the price of inserting in the middle.

quiz.q: You keep 30 students' marks in an array and read marks[17] instantly. What makes that instant read possible?
options: The array keeps a sorted copy of every element
The array searches itself in logarithmic steps
The compiler keeps a table of every index
The address is computed from the index and element size
quiz.why: Because the elements sit next to each other, the address of arr[i] is calculated directly, so the read is constant time.

quiz.q: In a 2D array a[4][5] stored in row-major order, which element comes immediately after a[2][4]?
quiz.why: Row 2 ends at column 4 (5 columns means 0 to 4), so the next element is the first column of the next row, a[3][0].

card.examTip: Write the addressing formula for a 2D array in row-major order; it is a standard 5-mark sub-question.

topics.title: Searching: Linear Search and Binary Search
topics.definition: Searching means finding the position of a target value in a collection; linear search checks items one by one, binary search halves a sorted list each time.

children.title: Linear search
children.definition: Compares the target with each element in turn; works on unsorted data and costs O(n).

children.title: Binary search
children.definition: Repeatedly halves a sorted array; costs O(log n) but requires sorted input.

children.title: Complexity comparison
children.definition: For a lakh records linear search may need a lakh comparisons while binary search needs about 17.

children.title: Which search to use
children.definition: Use linear search for small or unsorted data and binary search for large sorted data.

card.explanation: Linear search works on any array, sorted or not, and needs at most n comparisons, so it is O(n). Binary search needs the array sorted, then compares with the middle element and throws away half the list each step, giving O(log n). For small lists the difference is small, but for a lakh of records binary search finishes in about 17 steps while linear search may need a lakh. Binary search can be written with a loop or recursively, and the recursive version costs extra stack space.
card.example: To find a word in a dictionary you do not read page by page; you open the middle and decide which half to keep. That is binary search. Reading from page one is linear search.

quiz.q: Binary search requires the array to be:
options: Linked
Circular
Empty
Sorted
quiz.why: It decides which half to discard, so order is essential.

quiz.q: Worst case comparisons in linear search for n items:
options: log n
n
quiz.why: In the worst case every element must be checked once, so O(n).

quiz.q: Which statement about the two searches is NOT correct?
options: Binary search throws away half the list each step
Binary search needs about 17 steps for a lakh of records
Linear search beats binary search on large sorted data
Linear search works on sorted and unsorted arrays
quiz.why: On large sorted data binary search finishes in about 17 steps while linear search may need a lakh, so linear search is slower.

quiz.q: You have a sorted list of 1,000 student names and must find one name quickly. What does the card recommend, and why?
options: Binary search, because it needs about 10 steps
Linear search, because the list is already sorted
Binary search, because it also works on unsorted data
Linear search, because it compares fewer items
quiz.why: Halving 1,000 items takes about 10 comparisons, which is why binary search is the choice for a large sorted list.

quiz.q: About how many comparisons does binary search need in the worst case for 1,024 sorted items?
options: About 32, since 1,024 divided by 32 is 32
About 10, since 2 raised to 10 gives 1,024
About 1,024, one comparison per item
About 512, half of the list
quiz.why: Binary search halves the list each step, so the worst case is log base 2 of 1,024, which is 10.

card.examTip: Always mention the sorted-input condition of binary search; skipping it is a common loss of marks.

modules.title: Linear Structures: Stacks, Queues and Linked Lists

topics.title: Stack: Definition and Operations
topics.definition: A stack is a linear data structure in which insertion and deletion both happen at one end called the top, so the last element added is the first one removed.

children.title: LIFO (Last In First Out) principle
children.definition: The rule that the element pushed last is the element popped first, because the top is the only open end.

children.title: push operation
children.definition: Adds a new element on top of the stack by first checking that the stack is not full.

children.title: pop operation
children.definition: Removes and returns the top element after checking that the stack is not empty.

children.title: peek or top operation
children.definition: Reads the top element without removing it, so the stack stays unchanged.

children.title: isFull and isEmpty checks
children.definition: Boundary tests that stop a push into a full stack (overflow) or a pop from an empty stack (underflow).

children.title: TOP pointer
children.definition: A single index that always points to the current top element and is set to -1 for an empty stack.

card.explanation: Both insertion and deletion happen at the same end, the top, so a stack behaves Last In First Out - like a pile of plates where you take the last one placed. push adds at the top, pop removes the top, and peek only reads the top. Before pushing you test isFull, and before popping you test isEmpty, which prevents overflow and underflow errors. One variable named top is enough to manage the whole stack.
card.example: Your phone's back button keeps the pages you visited; pressing back returns you to the most recently opened page first - exactly LIFO.

quiz.q: A stack follows which order of access?
options: FIFO - first in first out
LIFO - last in first out
Random access by index
Priority order
quiz.why: Both push and pop act at the top, so the newest element leaves first.

quiz.q: Which operation returns the top element without deleting it?
options: peek
isFull
pop
push
quiz.why: peek (also called top) reads the element only; pop is the one that removes it.

quiz.q: Which statement about a stack is NOT correct?
options: Insertion and deletion both happen at the top end
The last element added is the first one removed
peek returns the top element and also removes it
isFull and isEmpty are tested before push and pop
quiz.why: peek only reads the top element; removing it is the job of pop, which is why it is used to look without changing the stack.

quiz.q: A text editor must undo the most recent change first, every time. Which structure fits, and why?
options: A queue, because changes are removed in order
An array, because changes are stored in place
A linked list, because changes are searched by value
A stack, because the newest change is removed first
quiz.why: Undo needs last in first out, which is exactly what a stack gives when every edit is pushed and every undo pops.

quiz.q: A stack is kept in an array of size 10 and top is currently 9. What happens on the next push?
options: Overflow, because top has already reached MAX - 1
Underflow, because the stack is completely full
The element at index 9 is overwritten quietly
A second array is created automatically
quiz.why: The array holds indexes 0 to 9, so top == MAX - 1 means the stack is full and the next push is an overflow.

card.examTip: Draw the stack as a vertical column with the top pointer marked, then label push and pop - most stack answers are marked mainly on this figure.

topics.title: Stack Representation: Array and Linked List
topics.definition: A stack can be stored in a fixed-size array using a top index, or built from linked nodes where the head is the top of the stack.

children.title: Array representation
children.definition: Elements stay in contiguous memory, top is an integer index, and the size must be fixed in advance.

children.title: Linked representation
children.definition: Each element is a node with a pointer to the node below it, so the stack grows and shrinks as needed.

children.title: Comparison of the two
children.definition: The array is faster and cache friendly but fixed in size; the linked stack is flexible but needs extra memory for pointers.

card.explanation: With an array you reserve space in advance and keep an integer top; pushing means top = top + 1 and writing there. With a linked list, push creates a node whose next pointer is the old top, and pop removes that node - the head of the list is the top of the stack. The linked version never overflows until memory itself runs out, but every node pays the cost of one pointer. The array version is simpler and faster per operation when the maximum size is known.
card.example: A canteen that always serves exactly 50 plates uses a fixed tray pile (array). A courier company whose parcel count changes every day stacks parcels on a trolley and adds more room as needed (linked list).

quiz.q: A linked stack overflows only when:
options: the head pointer is NULL
top equals size - 1
the memory of the machine is exhausted
it holds 100 nodes
quiz.why: Nodes are created on demand, so there is no fixed capacity limit.

quiz.q: In a linked stack, the top of the stack is:
options: the node with the largest value
the tail node
the last node created
the head node of the list
quiz.why: Push inserts at the head, so the head is always the newest element - the top.

quiz.q: Which statement about the two stack representations is NOT correct?
options: The array version keeps one integer top index
The linked version pushes a node whose next pointer is the old top
The array version can never overflow once the size is chosen
The linked version spends one pointer for every node
quiz.why: A fixed array overflows as soon as top reaches MAX - 1, so the size must be chosen with the worst case in mind.

quiz.q: A canteen serves at most 50 plates in one sitting. Which representation suits the plate stack, and why?
options: An array, because the maximum size is known in advance
A linked list, because the count changes every sitting
A linked list, because it pays no cost for pointers
An array, because it grows itself once the pile is full
quiz.why: When the maximum is known, the array version is simpler and faster per operation, and it never wastes pointer memory.

quiz.q: For a stack stored in an array, the underflow test before pop is:
options: top == MAX - 1, meaning the array is full
top == MAX, meaning the top left the array
top == -1, meaning there is nothing to remove
top == 0, meaning the first cell is still free
quiz.why: With top starting at -1 for an empty stack, top == -1 is the signal that a pop would be an underflow.

card.examTip: State the overflow condition (top == MAX-1) and the underflow condition (top == -1) for the array version - they are worth easy marks.

topics.title: Stack Applications: Expression Conversion
topics.definition: A stack converts an infix expression, where the operator sits between operands, into postfix or prefix, where the operator sits after or before them.

children.title: Infix notation
children.definition: The everyday form A + B where the operator is written between its two operands and brackets are needed.

children.title: Postfix notation (Reverse Polish)
children.definition: The form A B + where the operator follows its operands, so no brackets or precedence rules are needed.

children.title: Prefix notation (Polish)
children.definition: The form + A B where the operator comes before its operands.

children.title: Operator precedence and associativity
children.definition: The rules that decide which operator acts first: ^, then * and /, then + and -, left to right for equal rank.

children.title: Algorithm for infix to postfix
children.definition: Print operands, push operators, pop while the stack top has greater or equal precedence, and empty the stack at the end.

card.explanation: Computers find postfix easier because the order of operations is already fixed by position, so no bracket or precedence checking is needed at run time. To convert, you scan the infix expression once: operands go straight to the output, an operator is pushed only after popping every stacked operator of higher or equal precedence, and an opening bracket is pushed while a closing bracket pops until it meets its pair. At the end the remaining operators are popped. The same idea with a small change gives prefix notation.
card.example: The expression A + B * C becomes A B C * + in postfix, because multiplication is done before addition - exactly what an exam calculator does internally.

quiz.q: What is the postfix form of A + B * C?
options: A B + C *
A B C * +
A B * C +
A B C + *
quiz.why: B * C is evaluated first and printed as B C *, then the addition of A gives A B C * +.

quiz.q: Postfix expressions need no brackets because:
options: operands are sorted
the stack removes them
operators are written first
the position of the operator fixes the order of evaluation
quiz.why: In postfix, evaluation order is unambiguous from the layout alone.

quiz.q: Which statement about postfix notation is NOT correct?
options: An operator is pushed only after popping higher or equal precedence
The operator is written after its two operands
Evaluation order is fixed by position, so brackets are not needed
Every operand has to sit inside brackets to be evaluated
quiz.why: Postfix works precisely because position settles the order, so brackets are unnecessary and carrying them is meaningless.

quiz.q: While converting the infix expression (A + B) * C, what does the closing bracket make the stack do?
options: Pop the + because its opening bracket has been matched
Push the * before the + can be popped
Pop every operator that is still on the stack
Push the bracket itself onto the output
quiz.why: A closing bracket pops operators until it meets its opening bracket, so the + goes to the output and the bracket pair is discarded.

card.examTip: Show the stack contents after every scanned symbol in a table - examiners give step marks even if the final answer slips.

topics.title: Stack Applications: Postfix Evaluation, Recursion and More
topics.definition: A stack evaluates postfix expressions by pushing operands and, on meeting an operator, popping two values to apply it.

children.title: Postfix evaluation with a stack
children.definition: Push every operand; for an operator pop two values, compute, and push the result, leaving one value at the end.

children.title: Recursion and the call stack
children.definition: Each recursive call stores its state (parameters and return address) on the system stack and is popped when the call returns.

children.title: Balanced bracket checking
children.definition: Push every opening bracket and pop for every closing bracket; a mismatch or a leftover means the expression is invalid.

children.title: Backtracking and undo operations
children.definition: A stack remembers the path taken so the previous state can be restored when a choice fails or the user presses undo.

children.title: Conversion of number bases
children.definition: Repeated division by the base gives remainders that are pushed and then popped to print the digits in the correct order.

card.explanation: Evaluation is the reverse of conversion: you scan the postfix string and use the stack as working memory. Each operand is pushed; each operator pops two operands, applies itself and pushes back one result, so a well formed expression leaves exactly one value on the stack. Recursion uses the same structure invisibly - the computer keeps every unfinished call on a call stack. Bracket matching, undo history and base conversion are further everyday uses of this one idea.
card.example: When you press Ctrl+Z in a word processor, the editor pops the most recent change off an undo stack and restores the document state before it.

quiz.q: Evaluating the postfix expression 5 3 + 2 * gives:
quiz.why: 5 + 3 = 8 is pushed, then 8 * 2 = 16.

quiz.q: Recursion is naturally supported by a stack because:
options: the compiler sorts the calls
recursion needs no memory
the calls are stored in a queue
each pending call keeps its state on the call stack
quiz.why: LIFO suits nested calls: the most recent call finishes first.

quiz.q: Which statement about postfix evaluation is NOT correct?
options: A well formed expression leaves exactly one value behind
Each operator is pushed onto the stack as it is read
Each operand is pushed onto the stack as it is read
An operator pops two values, applies itself and pushes the result
quiz.why: Operators are applied, not stored; only operands are pushed, and each operator consumes two values from the stack.

quiz.q: Ctrl+Z in a word processor restores the state before the most recent edit. Which structure is the editor using?
options: A queue, because edits are undone as they were made
A deque, because edits are undone from both ends
A linked list, because edits are searched by text
A stack, because the newest edit is undone first
quiz.why: The card's undo example is last in first out: every edit is pushed and every Ctrl+Z pops the most recent one.

quiz.q: Evaluate the postfix expression 8 2 / 3 + .
quiz.why: 8 divided by 2 gives 4, then 4 plus 3 gives 7; both operations happen in the order the operators appear.

card.examTip: For postfix evaluation, show the stack after each symbol as a column of values - that single table carries most of the marks.

topics.title: Queue: Definition and Operations
topics.definition: A queue is a linear data structure in which insertion happens at one end called the rear and deletion at the other end called the front, giving First In First Out order.

children.title: FIFO (First In First Out) principle
children.definition: The element that entered first is the element that leaves first, because the two ends are separate.

children.title: enqueue operation
children.definition: Inserts a new element at the rear after checking that the queue is not full.

children.title: dequeue operation
children.definition: Removes and returns the element at the front after checking that the queue is not empty.

children.title: front and rear pointers
children.definition: Two indices that track the two open ends; both are set to -1 in an empty queue.

children.title: Queue overflow and underflow
children.definition: Overflow is an enqueue into a full queue; underflow is a dequeue from an empty queue.

card.explanation: A queue keeps its two ends separate - new items join at the rear and old items leave from the front - so service order is strictly first come, first served. enqueue moves the rear forward by one, dequeue moves the front forward, and both check their boundary condition first. Because nothing is removed from the middle, a queue is the natural model for any waiting line. A simple array queue wastes the space at the front after deletions, which is exactly the problem the circular queue solves.
card.example: A ticket counter line: the person who joined the line first buys the ticket first, no matter how long the queue becomes.

quiz.q: In a queue, insertion and deletion take place at:
options: the same end called top
rear and front respectively
front and rear respectively
any position
quiz.why: enqueue adds at the rear and dequeue removes from the front, which produces FIFO order.

quiz.q: An empty queue is indicated by:
options: top = -1
front = rear = 0
front = rear = -1
front = 0, rear = -1
quiz.why: The standard convention sets both front and rear to -1 when no element is present.

quiz.q: Which statement about a simple queue is NOT correct?
options: It gives first in first out service order
Items can be removed from the middle when needed
Nothing is removed from the middle, so it models a line
Insertion happens at the rear and deletion at the front
quiz.why: A queue only ever touches its two ends, which is what keeps the service order strictly first come, first served.

quiz.q: A system serves requests in arrival order, but its array queue is full after a few days even though requests keep finishing. What is the cause?
options: The queue keeps no front pointer at all
FIFO order cannot be kept in an array
The array queue wastes the space freed at the front
The queue has been used as a stack by mistake
quiz.why: Deletions move the front forward and leave empty cells behind it, so the rear hits the end while free space still exists in front.

quiz.q: An array queue of size 5 has front = 2 and rear = 4. How many items does it hold?
options: 5 items, because the array is of size 5
4 items, because the rear counts from the start
3 items, at indexes 2, 3 and 4
2 items, at indexes 3 and 4 only
quiz.why: The queue runs from the front to the rear inclusive, so indexes 2, 3 and 4 hold three items.

card.examTip: Write the FIFO example of a printer queue first, then the operations - real examples fetch marks in the first paragraph itself.

topics.title: Circular Queue and Its Need
topics.definition: A circular queue is an array queue in which the rear wraps around to the beginning using modulo arithmetic, so space freed at the front is reused.

children.title: Drawback of a linear array queue
children.definition: After deletions the front space is never reused, so the queue reports overflow while empty cells still exist - the false overflow problem.

children.title: Circular increment formula
children.definition: Instead of rear + 1, the next position is computed as rear = (rear + 1) % size, which wraps the index to 0 at the end.

children.title: Full and empty conditions
children.definition: The queue is full when (rear + 1) % size == front, and empty when front == -1; the full test deliberately leaves one cell free.

children.title: Counting the elements
children.definition: The number of items is (rear - front + size) % size plus one adjustment, which removes the need for a separate counter.

card.explanation: In a plain array queue, once the rear reaches the last index the queue is declared full even if deletions have left empty cells at the front - that is false overflow. The circular queue treats the array as a ring: the rear jumps back to index 0 when it passes the end, so freed cells are reused and no space is wasted. The price is that full and empty look identical when front equals rear, so one slot is deliberately kept empty to separate the two cases. Everything else, including the FIFO order, stays the same.
card.example: A 40-seat canteen where, after the first four students leave, new students occupy those same four chairs instead of standing outside.

quiz.q: The next rear position in a circular queue of size n is:
options: n - rear
rear + 1
(rear + 1) % n
rear - 1
quiz.why: The modulo operation wraps the index back to 0 after the last cell.

quiz.q: A circular queue of size n can hold at most:
options: n elements
n - 1 elements
n + 1 elements
2n elements
quiz.why: One slot stays empty so that the full condition can be told apart from the empty condition.

quiz.q: Which statement about a circular queue is NOT correct?
options: It keeps the same first in first out order as a plain queue
The rear wraps to the beginning using modulo arithmetic
It reuses the cells that deletions freed at the front
It removes the need to keep one slot empty
quiz.why: Full and empty would otherwise look identical, so one slot is deliberately left empty to tell the two states apart.

quiz.q: In a circular queue the rear sits at the last index. Where does the very next enqueue write?
options: At the last index again, overwriting it
At the index after the front, then stop
Nowhere, because the rear has left the array
At index 0, because the rear wraps around
quiz.why: The modulo step sends the rear back to index 0 once it passes the end, which is what makes the array behave like a ring.

quiz.q: A circular queue of size 5 has front = 3 and rear = 0 after wrapping. Where does the next enqueue write?
options: Index 0, overwriting the element at the rear
Index 3, because that cell is empty now
Index 4, because the array ends there
Index 1, because the rear moves on by one modulo 5
quiz.why: The rear advances with (rear + 1) % n, so 0 becomes 1, and the cell at index 3 is not touched because only the rear moves.

card.examTip: Mention false overflow while justifying the circular queue, then write the two conditions with the modulo formula - this is a very frequently asked 5-mark question.

topics.title: Priority Queue and Deque
topics.definition: A priority queue removes the element with the highest priority rather than the oldest one, and a deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends.

children.title: Priority queue
children.definition: Each element carries a priority; dequeue always takes the highest priority element, breaking ties by arrival order.

children.title: Implementation of a priority queue
children.definition: Commonly built with a heap, which gives O(log n) insert and delete-minimum, or with a sorted or unsorted list.

children.title: Deque (double-ended queue)
children.definition: A linear structure permitting insert and delete at both the front and the rear, so it generalises both stack and queue.

children.title: Input and output restricted deques
children.definition: An input restricted deque allows insertion at one end only while deletions happen at both; an output restricted deque does the opposite.

card.explanation: Normal queues serve customers strictly in arrival order, but many systems must let an urgent job jump the line - that is what a priority queue does. Elements are stored with a priority value, and deletion always removes the element with the highest (or lowest) priority, so the structure is not FIFO at all. Because a heap keeps the extreme value at the root, it is the standard implementation and gives logarithmic time for insert and remove. A deque is the other generalisation: it opens both ends, so it can behave like a stack, like a queue, or like neither.
card.example: In a hospital emergency room, a critical patient is treated before people who arrived earlier with minor injuries; a sliding-window maximum in data analysis is done with a deque.

quiz.q: A priority queue removes:
options: a random element
the oldest element
the newest element
the element with the highest priority
quiz.why: Priority decides removal order, not arrival time.

quiz.q: Which data structure is normally used to implement a priority queue efficiently?
options: Array
Heap
Stack
Circular list
quiz.why: A heap keeps the highest priority element at the root, giving O(log n) operations.

quiz.q: Which statement about a priority queue is NOT correct?
options: It removes the element with the highest priority
Every element is stored with a priority value
It always removes the oldest element, exactly like a queue
A heap is the standard efficient implementation
quiz.why: Priority decides the order, so an urgent job can overtake older ones, which is why a priority queue is not FIFO at all.

quiz.q: In an emergency room, a critical patient arrives after several minor cases. Who is treated first, and what does that show?
options: The critical patient, because a queue removes the last arrival
No one, because a queue cannot hold priority values
The critical patient, because removal is by priority
The minor cases, because they arrived earlier
quiz.why: This is the card's own example: a priority queue serves the element with the highest priority rather than the oldest one.

quiz.q: A heap-backed priority queue holds 1,000 items. About how many steps do insert and remove take?
options: About 1, because the root is always known
About 10, because a heap works in logarithmic steps
About 1,000, because every item is compared
About 500, because half the items are kept
quiz.why: Keeping the extreme value at the root gives O(log n) work, and log base 2 of 1,000 is about 10.

card.examTip: Compare priority queue and deque with the plain queue in a three-row table; the differences are what examiners look for.

topics.title: Applications of Queues
topics.definition: Queues model any first-come-first-served waiting line: CPU scheduling, printer spooling, buffers and breadth first search.

children.title: CPU and process scheduling
children.definition: The ready queue holds processes waiting for the processor, and round robin scheduling serves them in rotation.

children.title: I/O and printer spooling buffers
children.definition: Jobs are queued so a slow device such as a printer receives them in the order they were submitted.

children.title: Breadth First Search on graphs
children.definition: A queue stores the vertices discovered but not yet processed, which is what makes BFS explore level by level.

children.title: Resource sharing in operating systems
children.definition: Requests for a single shared resource, such as a disk track or a network line, are held in a queue.

children.title: Message and call centre queues
children.definition: Messages and calls are buffered in the order they arrive so that no request is lost while the system is busy.

card.explanation: Queues are the standard answer whenever requests must be handled in arrival order instead of instantly. Operating systems keep a ready queue of runnable processes, device driver software keeps a queue of pending jobs, and graph algorithms use a queue to explore level by level. Because all of these only ever add at one end and remove at the other, one data structure solves all of them. Recognising the FIFO pattern in a problem statement is usually enough to decide that a queue is needed.
card.example: Ten documents sent to one printer are printed one after another in the order they were sent, even though the printer is slower than the computer.

quiz.q: Which graph traversal depends on a queue?
options: Binary search
Dijkstra with a heap
Depth First Search
Breadth First Search
quiz.why: BFS keeps discovered vertices in a queue, which produces level-by-level order.

quiz.q: Printer spooling uses a queue because:
options: jobs must be printed in submission order
jobs must be printed by size
the printer is fast
the printer stores sorted data
quiz.why: Spooling preserves fairness by keeping FIFO order.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a queue application?
options: CPU scheduling of runnable processes
Printer spooling of pending documents
Breadth first search of a graph
Undo history inside a text editor
quiz.why: Undo history is last in first out, so it belongs to a stack; the other three all handle jobs in arrival order.

quiz.q: A graph must be explored level by level, finishing all neighbours of the start node before going deeper. Which structure does that, and why?
options: A queue, because nodes are processed in arrival order
A stack, because the newest node is processed first
A priority queue, because nodes carry weights
An array, because the graph is stored by index
quiz.why: Processing in arrival order keeps each level complete before the next one starts, which is why breadth first search is built on a queue.

card.examTip: Give three standard applications with one line each - CPU scheduling, printer spooling and BFS - and no examiner will ask for more.

topics.title: Linked List: Definition and Node Structure
topics.definition: A linked list is a linear collection of nodes scattered in memory, where each node stores a data value and a pointer to the next node.

children.title: Node structure
children.definition: A node has two fields: the information part holding the value and the link part holding the address of the next node.

children.title: Head pointer
children.definition: A single external pointer that marks the first node; losing it loses the entire list.

children.title: NULL terminator
children.definition: The last node stores NULL in its link field, which signals the end of the list.

children.title: Dynamic memory allocation
children.definition: Nodes are created with new or malloc at run time and freed with delete or free, so the size changes as needed.

children.title: No direct index access
children.definition: Items cannot be reached by position; you must follow the links from the head, so access is sequential.

card.explanation: An array keeps its elements side by side, so inserting in the middle forces everything after it to shift. A linked list avoids that by storing each element wherever free memory is available and joining them with pointers. The cost is that only the head is known, so reaching the k-th node means walking k links, and each node needs extra bytes for the pointer. Relying on one head pointer also means careless pointer handling can break or leak the whole list.
card.example: A treasure hunt where each clue gives the location of the next clue: the clues are in unrelated places, but the chain of pointers leads you through all of them in order.

quiz.q: Each node of a singly linked list contains:
options: an index and a pointer
only data
data and one pointer
two pointers only
quiz.why: One information field plus one link to the next node.

quiz.q: Access to the k-th element of a linked list takes:
options: O(log k)
O(k)
O(k squared)
quiz.why: Links must be followed one by one from the head, giving sequential access.

quiz.q: Which statement about a linked list is NOT correct?
options: Each node stores a value and a pointer to the next node
Any element can be read in one step, exactly as in an array
Reaching the k-th node means walking k links from the head
Nodes are scattered in memory and joined by pointers
quiz.why: Only the head is known, so there is no direct address arithmetic and a position must be reached by walking the links.

quiz.q: After weeks of use, free memory is scattered in small pieces. Why can a linked list still hold 10,000 records without moving any of them?
options: The list stores only the head and rebuilds the rest on demand
Each node goes wherever space is free and pointers join them
The list reserves one large block of memory in advance
The list sorts the nodes back into order after each change
quiz.why: Nodes do not have to sit next to each other, so scattered free space is fine and only the pointers need rewriting.

quiz.q: How many links must be followed to reach the 5th node from the head?
options: 1 link
4 links
5 links
3 links
quiz.why: The head is the 1st node, so four hops over four links land on the 5th node.

card.examTip: Always draw the node as two boxes with an arrow, and mark NULL at the end - the diagram answers half the question.

topics.title: Singly, Doubly and Circular Linked Lists
topics.definition: Linked lists are classified by how their nodes are linked: singly, doubly, circular and doubly circular.

children.title: Singly linked list
children.definition: Each node points only to the next node, so traversal is possible in one direction and the last node points to NULL.

children.title: Doubly linked list
children.definition: Each node has both next and previous pointers, allowing two-way traversal and easy deletion when the node itself is known.

children.title: Circular linked list
children.definition: The last node points back to the first node instead of NULL, so traversal can continue around the ring endlessly.

children.title: Doubly circular linked list
children.definition: A doubly linked list whose first node's previous pointer meets the last node's next pointer, giving two-way circular movement.

children.title: Choosing between the types
children.definition: Use singly for least memory, doubly when backward movement or easy deletion is needed, and circular for round-robin repetition.

card.explanation: The three classic forms differ only in how many pointers a node carries and where the last pointer lands. A singly linked list is the cheapest but can only move forward, so deleting a node requires its predecessor. A doubly linked list adds a previous pointer, which allows backward traversal and O(1) deletion once the node is known, at the cost of one extra pointer per node. A circular list replaces the final NULL with a jump back to the first node, which suits applications that cycle forever, such as round robin scheduling.
card.example: A music player's next button alone is a singly linked list; next and previous together make it doubly linked; a 'repeat all' playlist behaves like a circular list.

quiz.q: Which list allows traversal in both directions?
options: Singly linked list
Doubly linked list
Circular singly linked list
Array
quiz.why: Only the doubly linked node stores a previous pointer.

quiz.q: In a circular linked list, the last node's pointer:
options: points to itself
points to the first node
points to the middle node
is NULL
quiz.why: The ring is closed by linking the last node back to the first.

quiz.q: Which statement about the forms of linked list is NOT correct?
options: A doubly linked list stores a previous pointer as well
A circular linked list ends with NULL in its last node
Round robin scheduling suits a circular linked list
A singly linked list can only be traversed forward
quiz.why: The last node of a circular list points back to the first node instead of holding NULL, which is what closes the ring.

quiz.q: A music player must support next and previous, and deleting the current song should not mean walking from the start. Which form fits?
options: A circular list, because it never reaches an end
An array, because songs are reached by position
A doubly linked list, because the previous pointer is there
A singly linked list, because it saves a pointer per song
quiz.why: Carrying a previous pointer gives backward movement and constant-time deletion once the node is known, which is the two things asked for.

quiz.q: How many pointer fields does a node of a doubly linked list carry?
options: None, because the list keeps an index array
Two, one to the next node and one to the previous
One, pointing to the next node only
Three, one for each direction and one to the head
quiz.why: The extra previous pointer is exactly the memory cost that buys backward traversal and O(1) deletion.

card.examTip: Draw all three forms side by side with arrows, including the circular one closing into a ring - this diagram is the answer itself.

topics.title: Linked List Operations and Their Complexity
topics.definition: The standard operations on a linked list are traversal, insertion, deletion, search and counting, each with its own time cost.

children.title: Traversal
children.definition: Visit each node once by following the links, which is O(n) and the basis of every other operation.

children.title: Insertion at the beginning
children.definition: Create a node, point it at the current head and move the head; O(1) because no walking is needed.

children.title: Insertion at the end or after a node
children.definition: Requires reaching that node first, so it costs O(n) unless a tail pointer is maintained.

children.title: Deletion of a node
children.definition: Bypass the node with its predecessor's pointer and free the memory; O(1) if the node or its predecessor is known.

children.title: Search and count
children.definition: Both scan the list sequentially, so both are O(n) in the worst case.

card.explanation: All linked list work is built on one loop that walks from head to NULL. Because of that walk, operations near the head are cheap - inserting at the front is O(1) - while anything that needs a particular position costs O(n). Deletion itself is just pointer surgery, but finding the node to delete is the expensive part, which is why a doubly linked list helps. Comparing this with arrays shows the trade-off clearly: arrays win on random access, linked lists win on insertion and deletion in the middle.
card.example: Adding a new student at the front of a roll-call register takes one step; finding roll number 57 in the same register means reading through the earlier names.

quiz.q: Inserting a node at the beginning of a singly linked list is:
options: O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(n)
quiz.why: Only the head pointer and one new node are touched.

quiz.q: Why is deletion in the middle of a linked list usually described as O(n)?
options: The list must be reversed
Pointers need sorting
The predecessor must be located by traversal
Memory is copied
quiz.why: Reaching the position is the costly part, not the pointer change.

quiz.q: Which statement about the cost of linked list operations is NOT correct?
options: Searching for a value by comparison is constant time
Finding the predecessor is the costly part in a singly linked list
Inserting at the front of the list is constant time
Deleting a known node is constant time in a doubly linked list
quiz.why: A search has to walk the links until the value appears, so it costs O(n) even though the deletion that follows may be O(1).

quiz.q: Your program deletes a given roll number from a long singly linked list. What is the dominant cost?
options: Recounting the length of the list every time
Walking from the head to find its predecessor
Shifting all later records one place left
Copying the whole list into a new array
quiz.why: Pointer surgery itself is cheap; the expensive part is the traversal that locates the node before it, which is why a doubly linked list helps.

quiz.q: A singly linked list holds 1,000 nodes. About how many nodes must be visited to insert a new node after node 900?
options: About 100, counting backwards from the end
About 10, using binary halving steps
1, because insertion is always constant time
About 900, walking from the head to that node
quiz.why: Insertion is only constant time at the front; reaching a particular position needs the walk from the head, about 900 nodes here.

card.examTip: Tabulate the time complexity of insert, delete and search for a linked list against an array - this comparison appears almost every year.

topics.title: Applications of Linked Lists, Arrays versus Linked Lists
topics.definition: Linked lists are used wherever data grows or shrinks unpredictably: polynomials, sparse matrices, free memory lists, stacks, queues and hash chains.

children.title: Polynomial representation
children.definition: Each node stores a coefficient and an exponent, so only the non-zero terms of a polynomial occupy memory.

children.title: Sparse matrix representation
children.definition: Only the non-zero elements are stored as nodes with row, column and value, which saves large amounts of memory.

children.title: Free space and memory management
children.definition: The operating system keeps available memory blocks as a linked list of free nodes.

children.title: Implementing stacks, queues and hash tables
children.definition: Linked nodes give these structures unlimited size; chaining resolves hash collisions with one list per bucket.

children.title: Array versus linked list
children.definition: Arrays give O(1) index access and less memory per element but fixed size and costly middle insertion; linked lists give flexible size and cheap insertion but sequential access and extra pointer memory.

card.explanation: The strength of a linked list is that nothing has to move when the data changes - only pointers are rewritten, and the size is limited only by free memory. That makes it the natural choice for dynamic collections such as polynomials, sparse matrices and hash chains, and it is how stacks and queues are often built when their maximum size is unknown. The trade-off is sequential access and one extra pointer per element. Choosing between an array and a linked list is therefore a question about which operation dominates in the application.
card.example: A campus WiFi user list changes every few minutes as students connect and disconnect; a linked list simply adds and removes nodes instead of rebuilding the whole list.

quiz.q: Storing a polynomial as a linked list saves memory because:
options: coefficients are compressed
it allows random access
only non-zero terms are stored
it is sorted automatically
quiz.why: Nodes exist only for terms that actually appear, so zeros cost nothing.

quiz.q: Which operation is faster in an array than in a linked list?
options: Insert at the front
Access the 100th element
Delete the head
Grow beyond its size
quiz.why: Arrays compute the address directly, giving O(1) random access.

quiz.q: Which statement about choosing between arrays and linked lists is NOT correct?
options: Linked lists suit collections whose size changes often
A linked list never has to move its elements
An array gives direct access to any index
A linked list uses less memory per element than an array
quiz.why: Every node pays for a pointer field, so a linked list uses more memory per element than an array of the same values.

quiz.q: A polynomial has 12 non-zero terms out of 500 possible powers. Why is a linked list the better store?
options: Only the non-zero terms are stored, saving memory
Linked lists always answer lookups faster than arrays
Arrays cannot store more than ten terms in a row
Linked lists sort the terms automatically as they arrive
quiz.why: Storing only the terms that exist avoids 488 empty slots, which is exactly the sparse-data case the card names.

quiz.q: An array of 1,000 integers and a linked list of 1,000 nodes hold the same values. Which one needs more memory?
options: Neither, because both hold plain numbers only
The linked list, because every node stores a pointer
The array, because it keeps its values side by side
Both need exactly the same amount of memory
quiz.why: The linked list carries one extra pointer per element, which is the memory trade-off accepted for not moving data.

card.examTip: Prepare a five-row array versus linked list comparison table (access, insertion, deletion, memory, size) - it can be reused in almost any question.

topics.title: Tree Terminology
topics.definition: A tree is a non-linear hierarchical structure of nodes connected by edges with exactly one root and no cycles.

children.title: Root, parent and child
children.definition: The root is the single topmost node, a parent is a node with branches below it and its children are the nodes it connects to.

children.title: Sibling, ancestor and descendant
children.definition: Siblings share the same parent; ancestors lie on the path towards the root and descendants lie below a node.

children.title: Leaf and internal node
children.definition: A leaf (terminal node) has no children, while an internal node has at least one child.

children.title: Degree of a node and of a tree
children.definition: The degree of a node is the number of children it has; the degree of a tree is the maximum degree among its nodes.

children.title: Level, depth and height
children.definition: The level or depth of a node is its distance from the root, and the height of the tree is the number of levels or the longest root-to-leaf path.

children.title: Subtree and forest
children.definition: A subtree is any node together with all its descendants; removing the root leaves a forest of separate trees.

card.explanation: Trees describe hierarchies, so their vocabulary comes from family relations: parents above children, siblings side by side and leaves at the bottom. Two measurements matter in every tree question - degree, which counts children, and level, which counts distance from the root. These two numbers decide the shape of the tree and therefore how expensive searching it becomes. A tree with n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges, which is a fact worth remembering for numerical questions.
card.example: Your college's administrative chart - Vice Chancellor, then Deans, then Heads of Department, then faculty - is a tree with the Vice Chancellor as root.

quiz.q: The number of edges in a tree with n nodes is:
options: 2n
n
quiz.why: Every node except the root has exactly one edge connecting it to its parent.

quiz.q: A node with no children is called:
options: Root
Internal node
Leaf
Sibling
quiz.why: Terminal nodes with degree zero are leaves.

quiz.q: Which statement about tree terminology is NOT correct?
options: Every node except the root has exactly one parent
A node that has no children at all is called a leaf
A tree with n nodes always contains n edges
The degree of a node counts its children
quiz.why: A tree with n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges, which is the fact numerical questions in this topic are built on.

quiz.q: Your college chart runs Vice Chancellor, then Deans, then Heads of Department, then faculty. Which node is the root, and how do the edges compare with the nodes?
options: The Vice Chancellor, and edges are one fewer than nodes
The faculty, and edges equal the number of nodes
The Deans, and edges are twice the number of nodes
Any node, because a tree has no fixed root
quiz.why: The top of the hierarchy is the root and it has no parent, and every tree with n nodes carries n - 1 edges.

quiz.q: A tree contains 15 nodes. How many edges does it have?
quiz.why: One edge leads into every node except the root, so 15 nodes give 14 edges.

card.examTip: Label a diagram with root, level, degree and height before starting the answer - terminology marks are otherwise easy to lose.

topics.title: Binary Tree and Its Representation
topics.definition: A binary tree is a tree in which every node has at most two children, called the left child and the right child.

children.title: Left and right subtree
children.definition: Each node's two children head their own subtrees, and the two are not interchangeable - left and right have distinct meaning.

children.title: Array representation
children.definition: Nodes are stored by level in a linear array where the children of index i sit at 2i (or 2i+1 depending on convention) and 2i+1.

children.title: Linked representation
children.definition: Each node holds data plus left and right pointers, which uses memory in proportion to the number of nodes actually present.

children.title: Maximum and minimum nodes at a level
children.definition: Level i can hold at most 2^i nodes, so a binary tree of height h has at most 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes and at least h + 1.

card.explanation: The rule that a node may have at most two children makes the tree predictable, and that predictability is what algorithms exploit. In the array form the position of a node immediately tells you where its children live, so no pointers are needed, but gaps appear if the tree is not complete. In the linked form each node carries a left and a right link, which fits uneven trees neatly at the cost of two pointers per node. Because level i can hold up to 2^i nodes, the number of nodes at least doubles down the tree, which is why tree height grows only logarithmically.
card.example: A family tree limited to two children per couple behaves like a binary tree; 'left' and 'right' matter the same way birth order or twin order would.

quiz.q: The maximum number of nodes on level i of a binary tree (root at level 0) is:
options: i squared
i
2i
quiz.why: Each node can have two children, so the count doubles at every level.

quiz.q: Which representation wastes space for a skewed binary tree?
options: Array
Both equally
Neither
Linked
quiz.why: The array form must leave gaps for missing nodes, so a skewed tree leaves most of the array empty.

quiz.q: Which statement about binary tree representation is NOT correct?
options: Every node has at most two children, left and right
In the array form a node's children sit at fixed indexes
The linked form handles any shape without leaving gaps
In the array form a skewed tree wastes no space at all
quiz.why: A skewed tree fills only one side of each level, so the array form leaves the other half of every position empty.

quiz.q: A tree is a chain in which every node has only a right child. Which representation wastes memory, and why?
options: Neither form, because the tree has few nodes
The array form, because of the empty left child slots
The linked form, because it stores two pointers
Both forms equally, because the shape is the same
quiz.why: Index arithmetic doubles down the tree, so a chain occupies positions spread far apart and leaves most cells unused.

quiz.q: The most nodes a binary tree can hold on level i is 2 raised to i. How many nodes can level 3 hold at most?
quiz.why: 2 raised to 3 is 8, and counting from level 0 this is the fourth level down the tree.

card.examTip: Write the formulas 2^i per level and 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes total for a full binary tree; numerical questions come straight from them.

topics.title: Binary Tree Traversals
topics.definition: A traversal is a systematic way of visiting every node of a tree exactly once: inorder, preorder, postorder and level order.

children.title: Inorder traversal
children.definition: Left subtree, then root, then right subtree - visit order LNR; on a binary search tree this prints the keys in sorted order.

children.title: Preorder traversal
children.definition: Root, then left subtree, then right subtree - visit order NLR; used to copy a tree or create its prefix expression.

children.title: Postorder traversal
children.definition: Left subtree, then right subtree, then root - visit order LRN; used to delete a tree or produce a postfix expression.

children.title: Level order traversal
children.definition: Visits nodes level by level from left to right using a queue, which is breadth first search on a tree.

children.title: Reconstructing a tree
children.definition: Inorder together with either preorder or postorder fixes the unique shape of a binary tree.

card.explanation: Traversals exist because a tree is not linear, so there is no single natural order of visiting.
