Inorder puts the root between the two subtrees, preorder puts it first and postorder puts it last, and each has a matching use - sorting, copying and deleting respectively. Level order is different in style: it uses a queue and sweeps the tree breadth first, which is why it pairs with BFS. Names and visit orders must be memorised exactly, because examiners swap them deliberately while testing.
card.example: In a folder tree, deleting a directory (postorder) must remove the files inside it first; copying it (preorder) creates the folder before its contents.

quiz.q: Which traversal prints the nodes of a binary search tree in ascending order?
options: Inorder
Postorder
Level order
Preorder
quiz.why: Inorder visits left subtree, root and right subtree, which matches key order in a BST.

quiz.q: Level order traversal uses which data structure?
options: Queue
Priority queue
Hash table
Stack
quiz.why: A queue holds the nodes of the next level, giving FIFO level-by-level output.

quiz.q: Which statement about the traversals is NOT correct?
options: Level order sweeps the tree breadth first using a queue
Inorder places the root between its two subtrees
Preorder places the root before both subtrees
Postorder visits the root before its children
quiz.why: Postorder finishes both subtrees and visits the root last, which is why it suits deletion.

quiz.q: You are deleting a folder that contains files. Which order removes the contents before the folder itself?
options: Preorder, because the parent is handled first
Inorder, because the parent sits in the middle
Level order, because folder levels come first
Postorder, because children are handled before the parent
quiz.why: This is the card's own example: postorder reaches the root last, so the contents are gone before the folder is removed.

quiz.q: Level order traversal of a tree with n nodes works with a queue. How many times is each node put into that queue?
options: Exactly once, when it is discovered
Twice, once on discovery and once on finishing
Once per level of the tree
It depends only on the height of the tree
quiz.why: A node is enqueued when its parent is expanded and never again, which keeps the traversal linear in the number of nodes.

card.examTip: Memorise the three orders as LNR, NLR and LRN, then practise one tree drawn by hand - swapping these orders is the exam's favourite trick.

topics.title: Types of Binary Trees
topics.definition: Binary trees are classified by their shape: full, complete, perfect, skewed, balanced, expression, threaded and heap trees.

children.title: Full or strict binary tree
children.definition: Every node has either zero or two children - no node has exactly one child.

children.title: Complete binary tree
children.definition: All levels are completely filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right.

children.title: Perfect binary tree
children.definition: All internal nodes have two children and all leaves lie at the same level, giving exactly 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes.

children.title: Skewed binary tree
children.definition: Every node has only one child, so the tree degenerates into a linked list and its height becomes n.

children.title: Balanced and AVL tree
children.definition: A balanced tree keeps the heights of the two subtrees of every node within one, which AVL trees enforce by rotations and hold height at O(log n).

children.title: Expression tree
children.definition: Leaves hold operands and internal nodes hold operators, so inorder, preorder and postorder traversal directly give infix, prefix and postfix forms.

children.title: Threaded binary tree
children.definition: NULL pointers are replaced by threads pointing to the inorder predecessor or successor, which speeds up traversal without a stack.

children.title: Binary heap
children.definition: A complete binary tree with the heap order property - each parent is larger (max heap) or smaller (min heap) than its children.

card.explanation: These names describe shapes, and shape decides cost: a balanced tree of n nodes has height O(log n), while a skewed tree has height n and behaves like a list. Full means every internal node has two children, complete means the levels fill from the left, and perfect combines both with all leaves at the bottom level. Balanced variants such as AVL trees rebuild themselves with rotations whenever an insertion disturbs the balance. Expression trees and heaps are shape-based structures with a special purpose - evaluating expressions and supporting priority queues.
card.example: A tournament draw sheet that is completely filled to the final is a perfect binary tree; if one player receives a bye and the sheet collapses into a chain, it becomes skewed.

quiz.q: In a complete binary tree:
options: all leaves are at the same level
all levels are full except possibly the last, filled left to right
every node has one child
every node has two children
quiz.why: Completeness is about filling level by level from the left, which is why arrays can store them compactly.

quiz.q: A skewed binary tree of n nodes has height:
options: log n
n
n squared
quiz.why: One child per node means the tree becomes a chain of n levels.

quiz.q: Which statement about the types of binary tree is NOT correct?
options: Perfect means every leaf lies on the bottom level
Full means every internal node has two children
Complete means the last level fills from the left
Skewed means the tree stays balanced as it grows
quiz.why: A skewed tree is the opposite of balanced: it collapses to one side, so its height becomes n and it behaves like a list.

quiz.q: One player gets a bye and the tournament sheet collapses into a chain of single matches. What has the tree become, and why does it matter?
options: Balanced, because the height stays logarithmic
Skewed, so its height is n and search behaves like a list
Complete, so every level is filled from the left
Perfect, because every leaf is on the bottom level
quiz.why: A chain is the skewed shape, and losing the balance turns a logarithmic search into a linear scan.

quiz.q: A perfect binary tree has all its leaves on the bottom level. How many nodes does a perfect tree of height 3 hold?
quiz.why: A perfect tree of height h holds 2 raised to h plus 1, minus 1, so height 3 gives 16 - 1 = 15 nodes.

card.examTip: Draw one small example for each type - full, complete, perfect, skewed - and note where the definitions differ; that is where marks are lost.

topics.title: Applications of Trees
topics.definition: Trees are used wherever data or work is hierarchical: searching, indexing, expression evaluation, compression, files and decisions.

children.title: Searching and dictionaries
children.definition: A binary search tree keeps keys ordered so search, insert and delete cost O(log n) when the tree is balanced.

children.title: Database indexing
children.definition: B-trees and B+ trees keep disk blocks sorted with a shallow, wide shape, so a record is found in very few disk reads.

children.title: Expression evaluation and compilation
children.definition: Expression trees and syntax trees let a compiler evaluate arithmetic and check the grammar of a program.

children.title: File systems and organisation charts
children.definition: Directories, company hierarchies and classification schemes are naturally stored as trees.

children.title: Data compression with Huffman trees
children.definition: Frequent characters get short codes in a binary tree so the encoded file becomes smaller.

children.title: Decision trees and priority queues
children.definition: Decision trees model choices in machine learning and expert systems, while heaps implement priority queues.

card.explanation: Trees earn their place because they turn a linear scan into a short walk down a hierarchy of comparisons. Ordered trees give logarithmic search, which is exactly what database indexes and dictionaries need, and B+ trees extend that idea to disk blocks. Expression trees let a compiler evaluate and rewrite formulas, and Huffman trees compress data by giving frequent symbols shorter codes. Wherever the data itself is hierarchical - folders, organisations, classifications - a tree is the honest model rather than a convenience.
card.example: Searching a contact list of a lakh names: a phone book tree finds the name in about 17 comparisons, while checking names one by one could need a lakh.

quiz.q: Database indexes are usually built with which tree type?
options: AVL tree
B+ tree
Threaded binary tree
Expression tree
quiz.why: B+ trees are shallow and keep many keys per node, which suits slow disk reads.

quiz.q: Huffman trees are used for:
options: Sorting numbers
Data compression
Graph colouring
Memory paging
quiz.why: They assign shorter codes to more frequent characters.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an application of trees?
options: Database indexing with B+ trees
Data compression with Huffman trees
Keeping process queues for round robin scheduling
Expression evaluation inside a compiler
quiz.why: Round robin scheduling is a first come first served rotation, so it belongs to a circular queue rather than a tree.

quiz.q: A phone book tree finds one name among a lakh in about 17 comparisons. Why is that possible?
options: Each comparison discards about half of the names left
The tree keeps the names in ten fixed buckets
The tree checks every name but does it faster
The tree remembers the last name you searched
quiz.why: Searching down a balanced tree halves the remaining candidates at every step, which is what makes 17 comparisons enough for a lakh.

quiz.q: A balanced search tree holds one million names. About how many comparisons does one lookup need?
options: About 5
About 20
About 1,000
About 100,000
quiz.why: Halving a million takes about 20 steps, since 2 raised to 20 is a little more than a million.

card.examTip: Give at least five different applications with one line each - search, indexing, compression, file systems, decision making.

topics.title: Graph Terminology and Types
topics.definition: A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges, used to model any network of relationships, with no root and no hierarchy.

children.title: Vertex and edge
children.definition: Vertices (or nodes) are the objects and edges are the connections between pairs of them.

children.title: Directed and undirected graph
children.definition: An undirected edge works both ways while a directed edge (arc) has a direction, so a one-way road versus a two-way road.

children.title: Weighted graph
children.definition: Each edge carries a number such as distance, cost or time, which is what shortest path problems need.

children.title: Degree of a vertex
children.definition: The number of edges touching a vertex; in a directed graph we separately count in-degree and out-degree.

children.title: Path, cycle and connectedness
children.definition: A path is a sequence of adjacent vertices, a cycle returns to the starting vertex, and a graph is connected if a path exists between every pair of vertices.

children.title: Component and forest
children.definition: A connected component is a maximal connected part of the graph; a graph with no cycles is a forest, and a connected forest is a tree.

children.title: Other special types
children.definition: A multigraph allows parallel edges, a self-loop joins a vertex to itself, a simple graph has neither, and a bipartite graph splits vertices into two sets with edges only between the sets.

card.explanation: Graphs drop the tree restrictions: there is no root, a vertex may connect to any number of others, and cycles are allowed. That freedom is what makes graphs the right model for roads, friendships, circuits and course prerequisites. The vocabulary that matters most is direction (one-way or two-way), weight (cost on an edge) and connectivity (whether everything is reachable). Trees are a special case - a connected graph with exactly n - 1 edges and no cycles.
card.example: A metro map is a graph: stations are vertices, tracks are edges, interchange stations have a high degree, and a route that returns to the start is a cycle.

quiz.q: In a directed graph, the number of edges entering a vertex is its:
options: in-degree
weight
degree
out-degree
quiz.why: In-degree counts incoming edges, out-degree counts outgoing ones.

quiz.q: A connected graph with n vertices and no cycles has how many edges?
options: n
2n
quiz.why: That is exactly the definition of a tree, which is a special graph.

quiz.q: Which statement about graphs is NOT correct?
options: A graph may contain cycles and has no root vertex
The in-degree of a vertex counts edges entering it
A connected graph with n vertices and no cycles has n edges
An edge weight represents a cost or a distance
quiz.why: No-cycle connectivity is the definition of a tree, and a tree with n vertices has n - 1 edges, not n.

quiz.q: A metro map shows stations and tracks, and one route brings you back to the station you started from. What does that route show?
options: A spanning tree with no other edges present
A directed acyclic structure with no return
A cycle, which a tree is not allowed to contain
A root, which every graph must contain
quiz.why: Returning to the starting vertex is a cycle, and dropping the no-cycle rule is exactly what separates a graph from a tree.

quiz.q: A connected graph has 12 vertices and no cycles. How many edges does it have?
quiz.why: A connected graph with no cycle is a tree, and a tree always has one edge fewer than its vertices.

card.examTip: Start the answer by distinguishing a graph from a tree - no root, cycles allowed - then list the terminology with a small figure.

topics.title: Graph Representation
topics.definition: A graph is stored in the computer either as an adjacency matrix or as an adjacency list, sometimes also as an incidence matrix.

children.title: Adjacency matrix
children.definition: A V by V table where entry (i, j) is 1 or the edge weight if an edge exists; it uses O(V squared) space whatever the number of edges.

children.title: Adjacency list
children.definition: Each vertex keeps a list of its neighbours, which uses O(V + E) space and suits sparse graphs.

children.title: Incidence matrix
children.definition: A V by E table in which each column has a 1 or -1 marking the endpoints of one edge.

children.title: Which representation to choose
children.definition: Use a matrix for dense graphs and for O(1) edge existence tests, a list for sparse graphs and for quickly iterating over neighbours.

card.explanation: The representation decides the cost of everything that follows, so it is chosen with the graph's density in mind. A matrix answers 'is there an edge between these two vertices?' in one lookup, which is why weighted algorithms often use it, but it spends V squared cells even when few edges exist. An adjacency list stores only the edges that actually exist, so it is the practical choice for real networks that are sparse. Both forms can be used with the same traversal algorithms; only the running time changes.
card.example: A friendship network among a million users has only a handful of friends each, so an adjacency list is used - a million by million matrix would be absurd.

quiz.q: Space used by an adjacency matrix for a graph with V vertices:
options: O(V + E)
O(V squared)
O(E log V)
O(V)
quiz.why: The matrix always has V rows and V columns, regardless of the number of edges.

quiz.q: For a sparse graph, the preferred representation is:
options: Adjacency list
Incidence matrix
Distance matrix
Adjacency matrix
quiz.why: Adjacency lists store only the existing edges, saving both memory and traversal time.

quiz.q: Which statement about graph representation is NOT correct?
options: Both forms work with the same traversal algorithms
An adjacency matrix answers 'is there an edge' in one lookup
An adjacency list stores only the edges that exist
An adjacency matrix uses memory in proportion to the edges
quiz.why: A matrix always spends V squared cells whether the graph has many edges or almost none, so its memory does not follow E.

quiz.q: A friendship network has a million users with about 50 friends each. Which representation fits, and why?
options: An adjacency matrix, because it saves memory here
An incidence matrix, because it keeps weights
Neither, because a million vertices cannot be held
An adjacency list, because the graph is sparse
quiz.why: A million by million matrix would be absurd for 50 friends per person, and a list stores only the edges that exist.

quiz.q: An adjacency matrix is built for a graph with 1,000 vertices. How many cells does it use?
options: About 500,000, half of the square
Exactly twice the number of edges
One million, because the matrix is V squared
About 2,000, two cells for each vertex
quiz.why: Every vertex gets a row and a column, so 1,000 vertices need 1,000 x 1,000 cells regardless of the edges.

card.examTip: Show both representations for the same small graph side by side, then state the space complexity of each - that pair of sentences carries the answer.

topics.title: Graph Traversals: BFS and DFS
topics.definition: Breadth First Search explores a graph level by level using a queue, and Depth First Search dives as far as possible using a stack or recursion.

children.title: Breadth First Search (BFS)
children.definition: Start at a vertex, visit all its neighbours, then their unvisited neighbours, keeping discovered vertices in a queue and marking them visited.

children.title: Depth First Search (DFS)
children.definition: Follow one path as deep as possible, backtrack on dead ends, and use a stack (or the recursion stack) with a visited array.

children.title: Time complexity of both
children.definition: Each is O(V + E) with an adjacency list and O(V squared) with a matrix, because every vertex and edge is examined once.

children.title: Applications of BFS
children.definition: Shortest path in an unweighted graph, level order of a tree, finding connected components and testing bipartiteness.

children.title: Applications of DFS
children.definition: Cycle detection, topological sorting, finding articulation points and bridges, and solving maze or puzzle problems.

card.explanation: Both traversals visit every reachable vertex once and differ only in the order they choose to expand next. BFS expands the oldest discovered vertex first, which needs a queue and produces shortest paths when all edges cost the same. DFS expands the most recently discovered vertex first, which needs a stack or recursion and naturally produces backtracking-style exploration. The visited array is essential in both, otherwise cycles would cause the same vertex to be processed forever.
card.example: In a campus map, BFS finds the route with the fewest turns by spreading out in rings, while DFS is like exploring one corridor to its end before trying the next one.

quiz.q: Which data structure does BFS use?
options: Stack
Queue
Heap
Hash table
quiz.why: FIFO order gives the level-by-level expansion that characterises BFS.

quiz.q: The time complexity of BFS or DFS using an adjacency list is:
options: O(V)
O(E)
O(V + E)
O(V squared)
quiz.why: Every vertex and every edge is inspected exactly once.

quiz.q: Which statement about the two traversals is NOT correct?
options: BFS expands the oldest discovered vertex first
DFS expands the most recently discovered vertex first
BFS needs a visited array while DFS does not
BFS gives shortest paths when every edge costs the same
quiz.why: Both traversals need the visited array; without it a cycle would make them process the same vertex forever.

quiz.q: You must walk from the campus gate to the library with the fewest turns. Which traversal gives that route, and why?
options: DFS, because it keeps the turns on a stack
BFS, because it explores the deepest corridor first
BFS, because it spreads outward level by level
DFS, because it dives to the end first
quiz.why: Exploring in rings means the first time a place is reached it is reached with the fewest steps, which is the BFS guarantee.

quiz.q: A graph has 50 vertices and 200 edges, stored as an adjacency list. About how many steps does one traversal take?
options: About 2,500, because the cost is V times E
About 200, because only the edges are visited
About 50, because only the vertices matter
About 250, because the cost is V + E
quiz.why: Each vertex is expanded once and each edge is looked at once, so the total is 50 + 200 steps, written O(V + E).

card.examTip: Trace BFS and DFS on the same small graph, writing the visit order and the queue or stack after each step - the trace is what is being marked.

topics.title: Shortest Path Problem: Dijkstra's Algorithm
topics.definition: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from one source vertex to all other vertices when no edge weight is negative.

children.title: Single source shortest path
children.definition: The problem of computing the minimum total weight path from a chosen source to every other vertex in a weighted graph.

children.title: Greedy working of the algorithm
children.definition: Repeatedly pick the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance, then relax its neighbours by offering a shorter route through it.

children.title: Distance and visited arrays
children.definition: One array holds the best known distance from the source and another records which vertices are finalised.

children.title: Why negative weights fail
children.definition: The algorithm never revisits a finalised vertex, so a negative edge could later produce a shorter path it would miss; Bellman-Ford is used instead.

children.title: Time complexity
children.definition: O(V squared) with a simple array, or O((V + E) log V) using a priority queue (min heap).

card.explanation: Dijkstra works because once you have found the globally closest unfinalised vertex, no other route can reach it more cheaply - so that distance can be locked in. The algorithm then relaxes the neighbours, replacing their stored distance whenever a shorter route through the current vertex appears. This greedy certainty is exactly why negative weights break it: a negative edge arriving later could beat a distance that was already locked. The priority queue version is the practical implementation for large road and network graphs.
card.example: Google Maps computing the fastest route from your home to college, where each road segment carries a travel time as its weight.

quiz.q: Dijkstra's algorithm fails on graphs with:
options: negative edge weights
parallel edges
disconnected vertices
cycles
quiz.why: A negative edge could improve a distance already finalised, which the greedy choice forbids.

quiz.q: Dijkstra's algorithm is which type of algorithm?
options: Divide and conquer
Greedy
Dynamic programming
Backtracking
quiz.why: It repeatedly makes the locally cheapest choice of the nearest unfinalised vertex.

quiz.q: Which statement about Dijkstra's algorithm is NOT correct?
options: It works correctly on graphs with negative edge weights
A priority queue version suits large road networks
It finds shortest paths from one source to every vertex
It locks in the closest unfinalised vertex each round
quiz.why: A negative edge arriving later can beat a distance already locked in, which is why negative weights are excluded.

quiz.q: A road graph has one negative edge because it models a toll refund. What happens if Dijkstra's algorithm is run on it?
options: It runs faster because some edges cost less
It finds the shortest path exactly as usual
It needs a plain queue instead of a priority queue
The locked distances can be wrong, so it must not be used
quiz.why: Dijkstra's guarantee depends on distances never shrinking later, and one negative edge breaks exactly that promise.

quiz.q: Dijkstra's algorithm using a binary heap on V vertices and E edges runs in about:
options: O((V + E) log V), because each heap step is logarithmic
O(V squared) only, whatever the number of edges is
O(V + E), the same as a single traversal
O(E squared), because each edge is relaxed twice
quiz.why: A heap keeps the closest vertex available in logarithmic time, which gives O((V + E) log V) overall.

card.examTip: Solve one table with columns for vertex, visited and distance, updating it after each selection - examiners mark the table, not the final numbers.

topics.title: Topological Sorting
topics.definition: Topological sorting arranges the vertices of a directed acyclic graph in an order where every edge points forward, so each vertex comes before the ones that depend on it.

children.title: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) requirement
children.definition: Only a graph with directed edges and no cycles can be topologically sorted; a cycle means the tasks depend on each other and no order exists.

children.title: DFS based method
children.definition: Run DFS and push each vertex onto a stack when its recursion finishes; popping the stack gives a topological order.

children.title: Kahn's indegree method
children.definition: Repeatedly remove a vertex whose in-degree is zero, place it in the order and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees.

children.title: Cycle detection and output
children.definition: If some vertices remain unprocessed at the end, the graph has a cycle and no topological order exists; several valid orders may exist.

children.title: Time complexity
children.definition: Both methods run in O(V + E) with an adjacency list.

card.explanation: Topological sorting answers dependency questions: given tasks and prerequisites, what order lets you do everything? The graph must be acyclic, because a cycle would mean task A needs B while B needs A. The indegree method is intuitive - keep taking any task that has no pending prerequisite, then update the counts of what it unblocked. The DFS method achieves the same result by recording a vertex after all its successors have been finished. Because ties can be broken freely, a DAG usually has more than one valid order.
card.example: Course prerequisites: Data Structures before Algorithms before Network Security. Any order that respects every prerequisite is a valid topological sort of your study plan.

quiz.q: Topological sorting is possible only for:
options: Directed acyclic graphs
Complete graphs
Bipartite graphs
Undirected graphs
quiz.why: Any cycle would make the dependency impossible to order.

quiz.q: In Kahn's method, the next vertex chosen is one whose:
options: out-degree is zero
in-degree is zero
weight is smallest
degree is maximum
quiz.why: Such a vertex has no pending prerequisite, so it can be placed next.

quiz.q: Which statement about topological sorting is NOT correct?
options: A single DAG may have more than one valid order
It orders the vertices of a directed acyclic graph
Every edge in the result points forward
It can also order a graph that contains a cycle
quiz.why: A cycle means A needs B while B needs A, so no order can satisfy both and topological sorting is impossible.

quiz.q: A study plan says Data Structures before Algorithms, and Algorithms before Network Security. How many valid orders exist?
options: Three, one starting from each subject
None, because prerequisites make the plan cyclic
One, because the chain fixes a single order
Six, one for each permutation of the three subjects
quiz.why: A single chain of prerequisites leaves no freedom, so exactly one order satisfies every edge.

quiz.q: A project has 7 tasks and no prerequisites between them. How many of them have in-degree zero to begin with?
options: Only 1, the first task in the list
None, because every task has a prerequisite
6, because the last task has to wait
All 7, because nothing has to come before them
quiz.why: In-degree zero means no unfinished prerequisite, and with no prerequisites at all every task starts ready to run.

card.examTip: Mention explicitly that the graph must be acyclic, then show one complete trace - students often forget the requirement and lose a mark.

topics.title: Minimum Spanning Tree: Prim and Kruskal
topics.definition: A minimum spanning tree is a set of n - 1 edges that connects all vertices of a weighted graph at the least possible total cost.

children.title: Spanning tree
children.definition: A subgraph that contains all the vertices of the graph, is connected, and has exactly n - 1 edges with no cycles.

children.title: Prim's algorithm
children.definition: Start from any vertex and repeatedly add the cheapest edge that joins a tree vertex to a vertex outside the tree.

children.title: Kruskal's algorithm
children.definition: Sort all edges by weight and add them one by one, skipping any edge that would form a cycle, usually tested with a union-find structure.

children.title: Comparison and complexity
children.definition: Prim grows one tree and suits dense graphs with its O(V squared) array form, while Kruskal works on sorted edge lists, suits sparse graphs and costs O(E log E).

children.title: Applications
children.definition: Laying cable or pipelines, designing road and rail links, cluster analysis and network design at minimum cost.

card.explanation: A spanning tree connects everything with the fewest edges, and the minimum spanning tree chooses which edges so that the total weight is smallest. Both classic algorithms are greedy but differ in what they grow: Prim always extends the single tree, while Kruskal considers edges globally in increasing weight and avoids cycles. The cut property guarantees that these locally cheap choices produce a globally minimum tree when weights are distinct. Since n - 1 edges are needed no matter what, the only real decision is which ones.
card.example: Laying optical fibre to connect ten campus buildings: you must link every building, but you want the shortest total trench, so you pick the cheapest set of links with no loop.

quiz.q: A minimum spanning tree of a graph with n vertices has:
options: n + 1 edges
E edges
n edges
n - 1 edges
quiz.why: A tree on n vertices always has exactly n - 1 edges.

quiz.q: Which algorithm adds edges in increasing order of weight?
options: Floyd's
Prim's
Kruskal's
Dijkstra's
quiz.why: Kruskal sorts all edges globally and picks the cheapest usable ones.

quiz.q: Which statement about the minimum spanning tree is NOT correct?
options: Kruskal considers edges in increasing order of weight
It keeps a cycle in the tree to lower the total cost
It connects every vertex using n - 1 edges
Prim grows one tree outward from a start vertex
quiz.why: A spanning tree has no cycle by definition, and both algorithms explicitly reject an edge that would create one.

quiz.q: Ten campus buildings must all be linked by fibre with the least total trench length. What must the result be?
options: A complete graph with every pair of buildings linked
A shortest path tree measured from one building
A set of 10 links that forms one large cycle
A minimum spanning tree with 9 links and no cycle
quiz.why: Connecting everything at the lowest total cost is the definition of a minimum spanning tree, and it needs n - 1 links.

quiz.q: A network has 8 buildings that must all be connected. How many links does any spanning tree use?
quiz.why: A spanning tree always uses one link fewer than the number of vertices, so 8 buildings need 7 links.

card.examTip: Run both algorithms on the same graph and show the chosen edge set with total weight - comparing them in one table usually completes the answer.

modules.title: Algorithm Design Techniques: Divide and Conquer, Greedy Method

topics.title: Divide and Conquer: General Method
topics.definition: Divide and conquer solves a problem by splitting it into smaller instances of the same problem, solving them recursively, and combining their answers.

children.title: Divide step
children.definition: Break the input of size n into two or more smaller subproblems, usually of about half the size.

children.title: Conquer step
children.definition: Solve each subproblem recursively, or directly if it is small enough to be a base case.

children.title: Combine step
children.definition: Merge the subproblem solutions into the solution of the original problem.

children.title: Control abstraction
children.definition: A single skeleton - divide, recurse, combine - that describes every divide and conquer algorithm; only the split and merge rules change.

children.title: Recurrence relation
children.definition: The cost is written as T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), where a is the number of subproblems, b the shrink factor and f(n) the combine cost.

children.title: Classic examples
children.definition: Binary search, merge sort, quick sort, and multiplication of large numbers (Strassen's matrix multiplication).

card.explanation: The idea is old and simple: a hard problem of size n is broken into similar problems that are easier, and their answers are glued back together. Because the subproblems are of the same kind, recursion expresses the algorithm naturally, and the cost is captured by a recurrence like T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. Splitting into halves is popular because the depth of recursion then becomes log n, which keeps the total cost low. The technique pays off when combining partial answers is cheaper than solving the whole problem directly.
card.example: Finding the heaviest student in a class: split the class into two halves, find the heaviest in each half, then compare those two - the subproblems are smaller versions of the same job.

quiz.q: The general recurrence for a divide and conquer algorithm is:
options: T(n) = nT(n)
T(n) = T(n) + f(n)
T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
quiz.why: It has a subproblems of size n/b each, plus f(n) work to divide and combine.

quiz.q: Which step of divide and conquer is usually the most expensive?
options: Combine
Base case
Divide
Conquer
quiz.why: Merging the partial solutions often dominates, as in merge sort's linear merge.

quiz.q: Which statement about the divide and conquer method is NOT correct?
options: A problem is split into smaller instances of the same problem
Recursion expresses the method naturally
The cost is written as a recurrence relation
Splitting into halves makes the recursion depth n
quiz.why: Halving the problem at every step reaches the base case after about log n steps, not n, and that is why the method is cheap.

quiz.q: You must find the heaviest student in a class of 100. How does divide and conquer approach it?
options: Ask each student once and stop after the first answer
Split into halves, find each half's heaviest, compare the two
Compare every student's weight with every other student's
Sort the class by weight and then read the last entry
quiz.why: Each half is a smaller copy of the same job, and combining the two answers costs just one comparison.

quiz.q: An algorithm has the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. How many levels deep does the recursion go?
options: Two levels only, the left half and the right half
About log base 2 of n levels, halving each time
About n levels, one level for each element
About n/2 levels, one level for each pair
quiz.why: The problem size halves at every level, so the base case is reached after about log base 2 of n levels.

card.examTip: Write the three steps and the general recurrence as the first three lines of any divide and conquer answer; the rest of the marks follow from applying them.

topics.title: Binary Search as Divide and Conquer
topics.definition: Binary search finds a key in a sorted array by comparing it with the middle element and discarding the half that cannot contain it.

children.title: Precondition of sorted data
children.definition: The array must be sorted, otherwise discarding a half is not valid.

children.title: Recursive procedure
children.definition: Compare the key with a[mid]; if it is equal return, if smaller recurse on the left half, if larger recurse on the right half.

children.title: Iterative procedure
children.definition: Use low and high indices in a loop, updating them with mid - 1 or mid + 1, which avoids recursion stack overhead.

children.title: Analysis
children.definition: The recurrence is T(n) = T(n/2) + 1, giving O(log n) comparisons in the worst case and O(1) space iteratively.

children.title: Comparison with linear search
children.definition: Binary search is far faster for large sorted data, but it requires sorted input and does not work on linked lists efficiently.

card.explanation: Each comparison with the middle element eliminates half of the remaining items, so the search space shrinks from n to n/2, n/4 and so on until one element is left. That halving is why the cost is logarithmic - a million sorted records need only about twenty comparisons. The recursive and iterative versions are logically identical, but the iterative one avoids function call overhead. The sorted precondition is not optional: on unsorted data the algorithm silently returns wrong answers.
card.example: Looking up a word in a dictionary: you open the middle, decide which half the word lies in, and repeat - never reading every page.

quiz.q: Worst case time complexity of binary search is:
options: O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(n)
quiz.why: The search space halves at every comparison, so the number of steps is logarithmic.

quiz.q: Binary search cannot be used on:
options: a sorted list of numbers
a sorted list of strings
a sorted array
an unsorted array
quiz.why: Discarding a half is only valid when the data is ordered.

quiz.q: Which statement about binary search is NOT correct?
options: It works on an unsorted array if it is scanned twice
The recursive version pays extra function call overhead
It compares the key with the middle element
It discards the half that cannot hold the key
quiz.why: Halving only makes sense on sorted data; on an unsorted array binary search returns wrong answers instead of reporting a problem.

quiz.q: Binary search is run by mistake on an array that was never sorted. What happens?
options: It sorts the array first and then searches
It becomes slower but stays perfectly correct
It may return a wrong position without any error
It reports that the array is not sorted
quiz.why: The comparison only knows which half to drop, so unsorted data gives false guidance and a silently wrong answer.

quiz.q: Starting from 1,000 items, how many items remain after three comparisons of binary search?
options: About 500, because only the first half is dropped
About 1,000, because nothing is ever removed
About 250, because only two halvings have happened
About 125, because each step halves what is left
quiz.why: 1,000 halves to 500, then to 250, then to 125, which is why the search needs about log base 2 of n comparisons in total.

card.examTip: Write the recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 and solve it in two lines - the derivation earns more marks than the final O(log n).

topics.title: Merge Sort
topics.definition: Merge sort divides the array into two halves, sorts each half recursively and merges the two sorted halves into one sorted array.

children.title: Divide and merge steps
children.definition: Split the array at the middle, sort both halves recursively, then merge them by repeatedly taking the smaller of the two current elements.

children.title: Recurrence and analysis
children.definition: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives O(n log n) in the best, average and worst cases.

children.title: Space complexity
children.definition: The merge step needs an auxiliary array of size n, so merge sort is O(n) in extra space and is not in-place.

children.title: Stability of merge sort
children.definition: Equal elements keep their original relative order, which matters when sorting records by one field at a time.

children.title: Applications
children.definition: External sorting of files too large for memory, sorting linked lists, and counting inversions or other divide and conquer variants.

card.explanation: Merge sort trusts recursion completely: it sorts the left half, sorts the right half, and then assumes only one thing - how to merge two already sorted lists. Merging is easy and linear, comparing the front elements of both lists and always taking the smaller. Because the split is always at the middle, the recursion depth is exactly log n and every level does O(n) merging work, giving O(n log n) in every case. The price is the extra array needed for merging, and the benefit is guaranteed speed with stable output.
card.example: Two teachers each sort half of the answer sheets, then one helper merges the two sorted piles by always picking the smaller top roll number.

quiz.q: Time complexity of merge sort in the worst case is:
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n squared)
quiz.why: Each of the log n levels performs O(n) merging work.

quiz.q: The main drawback of merge sort compared with quick sort is:
options: It is unstable
It needs O(n) extra space
It works only on integers
It has quadratic worst case
quiz.why: Merging requires an auxiliary array, so it is not an in-place sort.

quiz.q: Which statement about merge sort is NOT correct?
options: It needs an extra array while merging
It splits the array in half and sorts each half recursively
Merging two sorted lists takes linear time
Its worst case is much worse than its average case
quiz.why: Merge sort splits exactly at the middle every time, so every case costs O(n log n) and there is no bad input.

quiz.q: Two teachers sort half of the answer sheets each. What does the merge step do, and what does it cost?
options: It re-sorts the combined pile from the beginning
It leaves the two sorted piles separate at the end
It compares the two front sheets repeatedly, in linear time
It compares every pair of sheets, in quadratic time
quiz.why: Each comparison removes one sheet from the front of a pile, so merging n sheets together takes about n comparisons.

quiz.q: How many levels of splitting does merge sort need for an array of 64 items?
options: 8 levels
6 levels
64 levels
32 levels
quiz.why: 64 halves to 1 in six steps, since 2 raised to 6 is 64, and that is why merge sort has log n levels.

card.examTip: Trace a small array through the recursion tree and show the merge at each level - the tree plus the merge lines is the expected answer format.

topics.title: Quick Sort
topics.definition: Quick sort picks an element as pivot, partitions the array so that smaller elements go left and larger go right, and then sorts both parts recursively.

children.title: Pivot selection
children.definition: The pivot may be the first, last, middle or a random element; random or median-of-three choices avoid the worst case.

children.title: Partition algorithm
children.definition: Two pointers move inwards, swapping misplaced elements until they cross, after which the pivot is placed at its final position.

children.title: Best, average and worst case
children.definition: Balanced partitions give O(n log n), while a very unbalanced split such as always picking the smallest element gives O(n squared).

children.title: In-place and unstable
children.definition: Quick sort uses only O(log n) space for recursion and needs no extra array, but equal elements may change relative order.

children.title: Merge sort versus quick sort
children.definition: Quick sort is usually faster in practice and works in place, while merge sort guarantees O(n log n) and is stable but needs extra space.

card.explanation: Quick sort does its heavy work before the recursion, not after: partitioning places the pivot exactly where it belongs and separates smaller from larger elements. If each partition splits the array reasonably evenly, the depth of recursion is log n and each level costs n comparisons, giving O(n log n). A bad pivot, as when the array is already sorted and you always pick the end element, creates partitions of size 0 and n - 1, which degrades to O(n squared). Choosing a random or median pivot makes that worst case very unlikely in practice.
card.example: Sorting a stack of exam papers by grade: pick one paper as a reference, place better papers on one side and weaker ones on the other, then repeat on each pile.

quiz.q: Worst case time complexity of quick sort is:
options: O(n log n)
O(n squared)
O(n)
O(log n)
quiz.why: Extremely unbalanced partitions make the recursion depth n with linear work per level.

quiz.q: The pivot in quick sort ends up:
options: in its final sorted position
in the middle always
removed from the array
at the beginning of the array
quiz.why: Partitioning puts every smaller element on the left and larger on the right, which fixes the pivot's place.

quiz.q: Which statement about quick sort is NOT correct?
options: Partitioning leaves the pivot in its final sorted position
A bad pivot can make the recursion depth as large as n
Its worst case is better than the worst case of merge sort
A random pivot makes the bad case unlikely in practice
quiz.why: Quick sort's worst case is O(n squared) while merge sort stays O(n log n) in every case, so quick sort's worst case is worse.

quiz.q: The array is already sorted and the code always picks the last element as pivot. What is the result?
options: Perfectly even partitions, giving O(n log n) work
The array is sorted with almost no comparisons at all
Quick sort notices this and switches to merge sort
Partitions of size 0 and n - 1, degrading to O(n squared)
quiz.why: The last element of a sorted array is its largest, so every partition is empty on one side and the depth becomes n.

quiz.q: Partitioning 100 elements costs about 100 comparisons. About how much do the two halves then cost together?
options: About 50, because the two halves are smaller
Nothing more, because the pivot is already placed
About 100 more, because every level costs n
About 10,000, because the halves are squared
quiz.why: Each level of recursion partitions the whole set once, so the work per level stays about n and the total becomes n times the depth.

card.examTip: Show the partition step with two pointers and state when the worst case occurs - the reason (already sorted input with an end pivot) is the marked part.

topics.title: Analysis of Recursive and Non-recursive Algorithms, Solving Recurrences
topics.definition: The cost of a recursive algorithm is expressed as a recurrence relation, and solving that recurrence gives its time complexity.

children.title: Step count of a non-recursive algorithm
children.definition: Count the basic operations as a function of input size, then keep only the highest order term.

children.title: Setting up a recurrence
children.definition: Relate the cost of size n to the cost of smaller sizes plus the non-recursive work, and state the base case.

children.title: Substitution or back substitution method
children.definition: Repeatedly expand the recurrence, spot the pattern, and sum the resulting series.

children.title: Recursion tree method
children.definition: Draw one node per subproblem with its cost, then total the cost level by level and multiply by the number of levels.

children.title: Master theorem
children.definition: For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), compare f(n) with n raised to log base b of a to read the answer directly in one of three cases.

children.title: Standard results to remember
children.definition: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 gives log n; T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives n log n; T(n) = T(n - 1) + 1 gives n.

card.explanation: Recursive algorithms are analysed by writing down what they cost, not by running them: the recurrence captures both the recursive calls and the work done outside them. Back substitution is the simplest manual method - expand a few steps, see the pattern, and sum the series - while the recursion tree shows the same thing as a picture of costs per level. The master theorem shortcuts all of it for the common shape T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) by comparing the combine cost with the growth of the subproblems. Exam questions usually expect one of these three methods plus the final O result.
card.example: Merge sort costs n work per level and there are log n levels, so the recursion tree is n wide at each of log n rows - total n log n.

quiz.q: Solving T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives:
options: O(n squared)
O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
quiz.why: Each of log n levels contributes n units of work.

quiz.q: The recursion tree method summarises an algorithm by:
options: totalling cost level by level
sorting the input
counting variables
running the code
quiz.why: Each level's total cost is added and multiplied by the number of levels.

quiz.q: Which statement about analysing recurrences is NOT correct?
options: The recursion tree adds up the cost level by level
The master theorem applies only to non-recursive code
A recurrence states the cost of a recursive algorithm
Back substitution expands the recurrence and sums it
quiz.why: The master theorem solves recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), so it is a tool for recursive algorithms.

quiz.q: Merge sort does n work on every level of its recursion tree and there are log n levels. What is the total cost?
options: n, because only one level is counted
log n, because only the number of levels counts
n log n, because each of the log n rows costs n
n squared, because the levels multiply together
quiz.why: Adding n work over log n rows gives n log n, which is exactly what the recursion tree method is for.

quiz.q: Solving the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 gives which complexity?
options: O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(n)
quiz.why: The subproblems grow to n while the extra work stays constant, so the total follows the number of subproblems, O(n).

card.examTip: Always state the base case along with the recurrence - a recurrence without its base case is considered incomplete.

topics.title: Greedy Method: General Method
topics.definition: The greedy method builds a solution step by step, always taking the choice that looks best at that moment, and never undoing a choice.

children.title: Feasible and optimal solution
children.definition: A feasible solution satisfies all the constraints; the optimal solution is the feasible one with the best objective value.

children.title: Objective function and constraints
children.definition: The objective function measures quality (profit, cost, distance) while constraints fix what is allowed.

children.title: Selection procedure
children.definition: A rule picks the next item to consider, for example highest profit, lowest weight or best profit-to-weight ratio.

children.title: Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
children.definition: The method succeeds only when a locally best choice can be part of a globally optimal solution and the problem has optimal substructure.

children.title: Control abstraction of the greedy method
children.definition: Start with an empty solution, repeatedly select the next best candidate, add it if it keeps the solution feasible, and stop when done.

children.title: Greedy versus dynamic programming
children.definition: Greedy makes one irreversible choice per step and is faster, while dynamic programming examines all choices and is needed when greedy fails, as in 0/1 knapsack.

card.explanation: The greedy method is attractive because it is simple and fast: there is no backtracking and no table of subresults, just a loop of locally best choices. That speed is only correct when the problem has the greedy choice property - taking the best-looking item now must never destroy the chance of the best overall answer. Fractional knapsack, minimum spanning trees, Huffman coding and Dijkstra's algorithm all satisfy it. Problems like 0/1 knapsack do not, and there a greedy choice can be clearly wrong, which is why dynamic programming is used instead.
card.example: Withdrawing the fewest notes from an ATM: take the largest note that still fits the amount, repeat, and you end up with the minimum number of notes.

quiz.q: The greedy method makes decisions that are:
options: made after full search
always globally optimal
locally best and never reversed
chosen randomly
quiz.why: It commits to the best available option at each step without backtracking.

quiz.q: Which problem cannot be solved correctly by a greedy choice alone?
options: 0/1 knapsack
Huffman coding
Minimum spanning tree
Fractional knapsack
quiz.why: An item must be taken whole or not at all, so a locally attractive choice can block the optimum.

quiz.q: Which statement about the greedy method is NOT correct?
options: It is correct for every problem, including 0/1 knapsack
It is fast because there is no backtracking
It always takes the choice that looks best right now
It never goes back and reverses a decision
quiz.why: 0/1 knapsack is the classic counterexample: items are indivisible, so a locally best choice can block the optimal answer.

quiz.q: An ATM must hand out 2,700 rupees using the fewest notes. Which approach does the card describe?
options: Take the smallest notes until the amount runs out
Halve the amount and withdraw it in two attempts
Take the largest note that still fits, then repeat
Try every possible combination of notes and pick the best
quiz.why: The greedy loop keeps taking the locally largest note that fits, and for Indian note denominations this reaches the fewest notes.

quiz.q: A greedy pass makes one decision for each of n items. Before any sorting, about how many decisions does it make?
options: log n decisions, halving the list each time
2 raised to n decisions, one per subset
n decisions, one for each item
n squared decisions, one for each pair
quiz.why: The greedy loop walks the items once and commits each time, which is what makes it linear before any sorting cost is added.

card.examTip: List the five greedy elements (candidate set, selection function, feasibility check, objective function, solution function) - this is a standard, mark-heavy question.

topics.title: Fractional Knapsack Problem (Greedy)
topics.definition: In the fractional knapsack problem, items can be cut, so the greedy rule of taking the highest profit-to-weight ratio first gives the optimal answer.

children.title: Problem statement
children.definition: Fill a knapsack of capacity M from n items with given weights and profits, maximising total profit when fractions of items are allowed.

children.title: Profit to weight ratio rule
children.definition: Compute pi/wi for each item, sort in decreasing order and take as much as possible of each item in that order.

children.title: Worked greedy steps
children.definition: Take whole items while they fit, and take only the fraction that fills the remaining capacity of the last item.

children.title: Why greedy is optimal here
children.definition: Because items are divisible, filling the knapsack with the best ratio per unit weight leaves no wasted capacity, so no exchange can improve the answer.

children.title: Time complexity
children.definition: Dominated by sorting the items: O(n log n).

card.explanation: The fractional version is easy because cutting items lets you fill every last unit of capacity with whatever is most valuable per kilogram. So you sort items by profit divided by weight, take whole items while they fit, and take a fraction of the item that crosses the capacity line. This exchange argument - any solution that does not follow the ratio order can be improved - proves the greedy answer is optimal. The problem becomes genuinely hard only when items are indivisible, which is the 0/1 knapsack of dynamic programming.
card.example: Filling a 5 kg shopping bag with rice, dal and ghee: pack the item with the best value per kilogram first, and if the bag is nearly full, take only the quantity that fits.

quiz.q: The greedy criterion for fractional knapsack is:
options: highest profit first
highest profit-to-weight ratio first
smallest weight last
highest weight first
quiz.why: Ratio ordering maximises value per unit of capacity, which is optimal when fractions are allowed.

quiz.q: Complexity of the fractional knapsack algorithm is:
options: O(n squared)
O(n)
O(n log n)
quiz.why: Sorting by ratio dominates the linear fill that follows.

quiz.q: Which statement about the fractional knapsack problem is NOT correct?
options: Sorting the items by ratio is the first step
Items can be cut, so a fraction of an item may be taken
The greedy rule works with profit divided by weight
The greedy answer is only approximate, never optimal
quiz.why: Because items are divisible, the exchange argument proves the ratio order is optimal, so the greedy answer here is exact.

quiz.q: A 5 kg bag must hold rice, dal and ghee, and ghee has the best value per kilogram. What does the greedy rule do as the bag fills up?
options: Takes ghee first, and only the quantity that fits
Takes equal quantities of all three items
Skips ghee because only whole items may be packed
Takes the cheapest item first to save money
quiz.why: The ratio order comes first and cutting is allowed, so the item that crosses the capacity line is taken in part.

quiz.q: An item has profit 60 and weight 4. What is its profit-to-weight ratio?
options: 56 per kilogram, the difference of the two
0.067 per kilogram, the weight divided by profit
240 per kilogram, the product of the two
15 per kilogram, which sorts it well
quiz.why: The greedy criterion is profit divided by weight, and 60 divided by 4 is 15 per kilogram.

card.examTip: Show the sorted ratio table, then fill step by step and state the final profit - and mention that greedy works only because items are divisible.

topics.title: Greedy Algorithms on Graphs: Prim, Kruskal and Dijkstra
topics.definition: The same greedy idea powers three classic graph algorithms: Prim and Kruskal for minimum spanning trees and Dijkstra for single source shortest paths.

children.title: Greedy view of Prim's algorithm
children.definition: Grow one tree by always adding the cheapest edge that leaves the current tree.

children.title: Greedy view of Kruskal's algorithm
children.definition: Sort edges globally by weight and add the cheapest edge that does not create a cycle, using union-find to test.

children.title: Greedy view of Dijkstra's algorithm
children.definition: Finalise the unfinalised vertex with the smallest tentative distance and relax its neighbours, so each step locks one shortest distance.

children.title: Single source shortest path
children.definition: Distances from one source to all vertices, computed correctly when all edge weights are non-negative.

children.title: Complexity comparison
children.definition: Prim O(V squared) or O(E log V), Kruskal O(E log E), Dijkstra O(V squared) or O((V+E) log V) with a heap.

card.explanation: All three algorithms look locally optimal yet produce globally optimal results, and the reason in each case is a cutting argument. Prim's tree can never be improved by a cheaper edge crossing the cut, Kruskal's sorted edge list cannot be improved by any lighter edge that avoids a cycle, and Dijkstra's finalised distance cannot be beaten because all remaining paths already cost more. The shared structure is a loop that repeatedly extracts the best remaining candidate - which is why a priority queue is the natural implementation. Note that Dijkstra, unlike the other two, requires non-negative weights.
card.example: Planning fibre links between campus buildings (Prim), picking the cheapest cable contracts overall (Kruskal), and finding the fastest route from your hostel to the department (Dijkstra).

quiz.q: Which of these three algorithms fails with negative edge weights?
options: Dijkstra's
None of them
Prim's
Kruskal's
quiz.why: Dijkstra finalises vertices greedily, which a negative edge could later contradict.

quiz.q: Kruskal's algorithm uses which structure to detect cycles efficiently?
options: Hash table
Stack
Union-find (disjoint set)
Queue
quiz.why: Union-find tells in almost constant time whether two endpoints are already connected.

quiz.q: Which statement about these three greedy graph algorithms is NOT correct?
options: Dijkstra works correctly with negative edge weights
All three repeatedly take the best remaining candidate
Prim grows one tree outward from a start vertex
Kruskal uses union-find to detect cycles
quiz.why: Dijkstra finalises a distance as soon as it is the closest, and a negative edge arriving later can still beat it.

quiz.q: You must find the fastest route from the hostel to the department on a road map carrying travel times. Which algorithm fits?
options: Either Prim's or Kruskal's, since both find routes
Dijkstra's, because it finds shortest paths from one source
Prim's, because it grows a tree across the map
Kruskal's, because it sorts the roads by weight
quiz.why: A single source with weighted edges and a destination is exactly the shortest path problem Dijkstra's algorithm solves.

quiz.q: Kruskal's algorithm sorts the edges before scanning them. For 300 edges, about how many comparisons does a good sort need?
options: About 300, since each edge is read once
About 90,000, since every pair is compared
About 8, since the depth is logarithmic
About 2,400, since a good sort is n log n
quiz.why: 300 edges need about 300 times log base 2 of 300, which is roughly 2,400 comparisons, and that sorting cost dominates the algorithm.

card.examTip: Compare the three in one table - problem solved, greedy rule, data structure used and complexity - since most questions ask for exactly this comparison.

topics.title: Scheduling: Job Sequencing with Deadlines
topics.definition: Job sequencing with deadlines arranges unit-time jobs with profits and deadlines so that the total profit of jobs completed in time is maximum.

children.title: Problem statement
children.definition: Each job takes one unit of time, must finish by its deadline and earns a profit; jobs that miss the deadline earn nothing.

children.title: Greedy rule
children.definition: Sort jobs in decreasing order of profit and place each job in the latest free slot before its deadline.

children.title: Feasibility check
children.definition: A set of jobs is feasible if they can all be scheduled within their deadlines; scanning slots from the deadline backwards keeps it feasible.

children.title: Worked example
children.definition: For jobs with profits 100, 50, 40 and deadlines 2, 1, 2, the greedy order takes the first and third, giving a total profit of 140.

children.title: Time complexity
children.definition: O(n log n) for the sort plus up to O(n squared) for slot searching, which can be reduced with union-find.

card.explanation: This problem is about limited time, so the greedy measure is profit rather than ratio: consider the most profitable job first. Each job must be placed somewhere, and putting it as late as possible keeps earlier slots free for others, which is what preserves feasibility. If no free slot exists before the deadline, that job is simply dropped. The sorted job order plus the latest-possible-slot rule produces an optimal schedule for unit-time jobs.
card.example: Exam week with four submissions due on different days and different credit weights: do the highest-weight submission first, and each one as late as its deadline allows so urgent small ones can fit in.

quiz.q: In job sequencing with deadlines, jobs are considered in order of:
options: increasing deadline
decreasing profit
shortest processing time
arrival time
quiz.why: Greedy picks the most profitable job first and then finds it a feasible slot.

quiz.q: A job is rejected during the greedy scan when:
options: its deadline is the largest
its profit is low
no free slot exists before its deadline
it is the last job
quiz.why: Without a free slot in time it cannot be scheduled, so it is discarded.

quiz.q: Which statement about job sequencing with deadlines is NOT correct?
options: Jobs are considered in decreasing order of profit
Each job is placed as late as its deadline allows
A job is dropped even when a free slot is available
The result maximises the profit of the jobs finished in time
quiz.why: A job is dropped only when no free slot exists before its deadline; if a slot exists, the job is scheduled there.

quiz.q: Four submissions are due on different days with different credit weights. How does the greedy scan schedule them?
options: Earliest deadline first, in the order they are due
Shortest job first, ignoring the credit weight
Alphabetical order, filling the first free day each time
Highest profit first, each as late as its deadline allows
quiz.why: Profit decides the order and the latest possible slot keeps earlier slots free, which is what protects feasibility.

quiz.q: Two unit-time jobs both carry profit, with deadlines 1 and 2. How many can be finished in time?
options: Both, but only if they run on the same day
Both, because there are two slots before the deadlines
Only one, because both jobs need day 1
Neither, because the deadlines are too close
quiz.why: The deadline 1 job goes into slot 1 and the deadline 2 job into slot 2, so both fit before their deadlines.

card.examTip: Draw the timeline of slots and mark each chosen job with its deadline - the timeline diagram is the answer examiners look for.

topics.title: Huffman Coding
topics.definition: Huffman coding builds an optimal binary tree in which frequently used characters get short codes and rare characters get long codes, reducing file size.

children.title: Fixed length versus variable length codes
children.definition: Fixed length codes use the same number of bits for every character; variable length codes assign fewer bits to frequent characters.

children.title: Prefix code property
children.definition: No code is a prefix of another, which makes decoding unambiguous without separators.

children.title: Building the Huffman tree
children.definition: Put all characters in a min-heap by frequency; repeatedly remove the two smallest, join them under a new node whose frequency is their sum, and continue until one tree remains.

children.title: Assigning codes and decoding
children.definition: Label left edges 0 and right edges 1; a character's code is the path from the root, and decoding walks the same tree from the root.

children.title: Complexity and applications
children.definition: O(n log n) with a heap; used in file compression such as ZIP, in image formats and in data transmission.

card.explanation: Huffman coding exploits the fact that in normal text some letters appear far more often than others, so giving every letter eight bits wastes space. The greedy rule merges the two least frequent characters at every step, which pushes rare characters deeper into the tree and frequent ones closer to the root. The result is a prefix code, so the 0 and 1 path to each character is unambiguous and no separator is needed. Because the greedy merge is provably optimal, no other prefix code gives a shorter average length for the same frequencies.
card.example: In an SMS, letters like e and a get short codes while z and q get long ones, so the same message needs fewer bits overall.

quiz.q: In Huffman coding, the two nodes combined at each step are the ones with:
options: equal frequency
highest frequency
lowest frequency
longest code
quiz.why: Merging the rarest characters first pushes them deepest into the tree, which minimises total code length.

quiz.q: A prefix code means:
options: every code has equal length
no code is a prefix of another code
codes start with 1
codes are sorted
quiz.why: This property makes decoding unambiguous while reading bits one at a time.

quiz.q: Which statement about Huffman coding is NOT correct?
options: The two least frequent nodes are merged at each step
Frequent characters end up deeper in the tree
The code is a prefix code, so no separator is needed
Frequent characters receive the shorter codes
quiz.why: Merging the rarest characters first pushes them deep into the tree, so frequent characters stay near the root with short codes.

quiz.q: In an SMS, the letter e appears far more often than q. What does Huffman coding do about that?
options: It gives e a shorter code and q a longer one
It gives both letters the same eight bit code
It removes the rare letters from the message
It gives q the shorter code because q is rarer
quiz.why: Shorter codes for frequent characters is the whole idea, and it lowers the average number of bits per character.

quiz.q: Five characters have frequencies 5, 7, 10, 15 and 20. Which two are merged first?
options: The 15 and the 20, the two largest
The 10 and the 15, the middle pair
The 5 and the 20, the extremes
The 5 and the 7, the two smallest
quiz.why: Huffman always merges the two lowest frequencies first, so 5 and 7 combine into a node of weight 12.

card.examTip: Show the frequency-sorted list, then every merge step in order and the final codes in a table - the merge order itself carries most of the marks.

modules.title: Dynamic Programming, Backtracking and Complexity Classes

topics.title: Dynamic Programming: General Method
topics.definition: Dynamic programming solves a problem by storing the answers to overlapping subproblems and reusing them instead of recomputing.

children.title: Overlapping subproblems
children.definition: The same smaller problem is needed again and again, so recomputing it wastes time.

children.title: Optimal substructure
children.definition: An optimal solution contains optimal solutions of its subproblems, so small answers can be combined into the big one.

children.title: Principle of optimality
children.definition: Whatever the first decision, the remaining decisions must be optimal for the state that results from it.

children.title: Memoization (top-down)
children.definition: Write the recursion naturally but cache each computed result, so repeated calls return from the table.

children.title: Tabulation (bottom-up)
children.definition: Fill a table iteratively from the smallest subproblems upward, which avoids recursion overhead.

children.title: Dynamic programming versus greedy and divide and conquer
children.definition: Unlike greedy it considers all choices, and unlike plain divide and conquer it reuses results of overlapping subproblems instead of solving them again.

card.explanation: Dynamic programming is the answer when a problem has two features: the best overall solution is built from best solutions of smaller pieces, and those smaller pieces keep repeating. A plain recursive solution would recompute the same states exponentially many times, while dynamic programming computes each state once and looks it up afterwards. Memoization does that lazily from the top with the recursion kept as it is, and tabulation does it eagerly from the bottom with loops. The cost is memory for the table, and the reward is turning exponential recursion into polynomial time.
card.example: Climbing a staircase of 10 steps taking 1 or 2 steps at a time: the number of ways to reach step 8 and step 9 is reused to find step 10, instead of counting from scratch each time.

quiz.q: Dynamic programming is preferred when a problem has:
options: negative weights
no solution
no recursion
overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
quiz.why: These two properties let stored subproblem answers be combined into the optimum.

quiz.q: Memoization differs from tabulation because it:
options: is always iterative
ignores subproblems
uses a table
works top-down and caches results lazily
quiz.why: Memoization keeps recursion but stores answers the first time they are computed.

quiz.q: Which statement about dynamic programming is NOT correct?
options: It spends memory on the table to avoid repeated work
It stores answers to overlapping subproblems
Memoization is top-down and tabulation bottom-up
It recomputes every state each time it is needed
quiz.why: Each state is computed once and looked up afterwards, which is what turns exponential recursion into polynomial time.

quiz.q: You must count the ways to climb 10 steps taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. What does dynamic programming do differently from plain recursion?
options: It converts the count into a greedy choice
It stores the counts for smaller steps and reuses them
It tries every order of steps again from the beginning
It guesses a pattern and multiplies it out
quiz.why: The counts for step 8 and step 9 are needed repeatedly, so caching them removes the exponential repetition of plain recursion.

quiz.q: A dynamic programming table has one state for each item and each capacity. For 5 items and capacity 10, how many states are there?
options: 15 states, because items and capacities are added
32 states, one for every subset of items
100 states, because the items are squared
50 states, because every item is paired with every capacity
quiz.why: The table is the product of the two dimensions, so 5 items across 10 capacities gives 50 states, written O(nW).

card.examTip: State the principle of optimality in the very first line, then write the recurrence and the table - this sequence matches the expected answer format.

topics.title: 0/1 Knapsack Using Dynamic Programming
topics.definition: In the 0/1 knapsack problem each item must be taken whole or left behind, so dynamic programming is used to choose the most profitable subset within the weight limit.

children.title: Problem statement
children.definition: Choose a subset of n items with weights wi and profits pi such that the total weight does not exceed capacity M and the total profit is maximum.

children.title: Recurrence relation
children.definition: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], pi + dp[i-1][w - wi]) when the item fits, otherwise dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w].

children.title: Table construction
children.definition: Build a table with items as rows and capacities as columns, filling each cell from the cell above and the cell above-left.

children.title: Backtracking the chosen items
children.definition: Walk back through the table: an item was included if the value differs from the row above, which reconstructs the optimal subset.

children.title: Time and space complexity
children.definition: O(nW) time and O(nW) space, reducible to O(W) space by keeping only one row; this is pseudo-polynomial, not polynomial in the input size.

children.title: Contrast with fractional knapsack
children.definition: Greedy by ratio fails here because an attractive item may leave no room for a better combination later.

card.explanation: Because an item cannot be cut, every decision is a yes-or-no choice, and a locally attractive greedy pick can spoil the remaining capacity - so all choices are explored and remembered. The state is simply 'best profit using the first i items with capacity w', and each cell either leaves the item out or includes it and adds the column shifted left by its weight. Filling the table row by row writes every one of those answers exactly once, and the last cell holds the maximum profit. Walking backwards through the table tells you which items were actually chosen.
card.example: Packing a 3 kg travel bag from items with weights 2, 2 and 3 kg and values 4, 5 and 6 - taking the 2 kg plus 1 kg is impossible because nothing can be cut, so the DP table compares whole combinations.

quiz.q: The 0/1 knapsack recurrence for an item that fits is:
options: dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w - wi]
dp[i][w] = wi + pi
dp[i][w] = pi + dp[i][w - wi]
dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], pi + dp[i-1][w - wi])
quiz.why: Either exclude the item, or include it and add the best of the remaining capacity from the previous row.

quiz.q: The complexity of the dynamic programming knapsack is:
options: O(n log n)
O(nW)
O(W squared)
quiz.why: The table has n rows and W columns, each filled in constant time.

quiz.q: Which statement about the 0/1 knapsack problem is NOT correct?
options: The state records the best profit for the first i items and capacity w
Greedy order by profit-to-weight ratio is always optimal here
The table is filled row by row and the last cell holds the answer
Each item is taken whole or left behind
quiz.why: Ratio greedy is optimal only in the fractional version; with indivisible items a good ratio can block a better combination.

quiz.q: Items weigh 2, 2 and 3 kg with values 4, 5 and 6, and the bag holds 4 kg. Why can the bag not be filled to exactly 4 kg?
options: Because the three values are all different
Because the table needs a fifth column
Because the capacity must be an even number
Because an item may not be cut into a fraction
quiz.why: The 0/1 rule allows only whole items, so 2 + 2 = 4 kg is used and the 3 kg item cannot be split to top up the last kilogram.

quiz.q: A knapsack table is built with one row per item and one column per capacity, for 4 items and capacity 8. How many cells does that give?
options: 64 cells, because the size is squared
16 cells, one for every subset
32 cells, four rows of eight
12 cells, four plus eight
quiz.why: Rows times columns gives 4 times 8, which is 32 cells, and that count is exactly why the algorithm is O(nW).

card.examTip: Draw the full dp table with rows as items and columns as capacities, then mark the included items by back-tracing - a table without the trace-back loses marks.

topics.title: Travelling Salesman Problem
topics.definition: The travelling salesman problem asks for the shortest tour that visits every city exactly once and returns to the starting city.

children.title: Problem statement
children.definition: Given a cost matrix between n cities, find a Hamiltonian cycle of minimum total cost.

children.title: Brute force and its cost
children.definition: Trying every tour needs (n - 1)! permutations, so even fifteen cities are beyond brute force.

children.title: Dynamic programming formulation
children.definition: Solve subproblems defined by 'shortest path from city 1 to city j visiting exactly the set S of cities', storing them by (j, S).

children.title: Complexity of the Held-Karp method
children.definition: O(n squared times 2^n) time and O(n times 2^n) space, which is far better than factorial but still exponential.

children.title: TSP is NP-hard
children.definition: No polynomial time algorithm is known, so in practice approximation and heuristic methods are used.

children.title: Applications
children.definition: Delivery route planning, circuit board drilling, school bus routing and warehouse picking.

card.explanation: The TSP is deceptively small: visiting every city once is easy, but visiting them in the cheapest order means comparing an astronomical number of tours. Dynamic programming improves the search dramatically by noticing that what matters for the future is which cities remain and where you currently are, not the exact order already travelled. That shrinks the problem into states of the form 'current city plus set of visited cities', which is exponential but far smaller than factorial. Even so, no polynomial algorithm is known, which places TSP among the NP-hard problems.
card.example: A delivery van must visit twelve shops and return to the depot; checking every possible order means billions of tours, so routing software uses dynamic programming or heuristics.

quiz.q: The number of distinct tours checked by brute force for n cities is about:
options: n squared
n log n
quiz.why: Fixing the start leaves permutations of the remaining n - 1 cities.

quiz.q: The dynamic programming state for TSP consists of:
options: the starting city
only the current city
current city and the set of visited cities
the total cost so far only
quiz.why: Those two pieces of information are enough to decide the rest of the tour optimally.

quiz.q: Which statement about the travelling salesman problem is NOT correct?
options: The tour visits every city once and returns to the start
Brute force checks about (n - 1) factorial tours
Dynamic programming solves it in polynomial time
No polynomial time algorithm is known for it
quiz.why: Dynamic programming shrinks the search to states of current city plus visited set, but that is still exponential, so TSP stays NP-hard.
