quiz.q: A delivery van must visit twelve shops and return to the depot. Why is comparing every possible order useless in practice?
options: The depot cannot be visited again at the end
Routes must be arranged alphabetically, not cheapest
Twelve cities mean billions of tours to compare
Twelve cities cannot fit in the computer's memory
quiz.why: The number of tours grows factorially, so eleven factorial orders is in the billions even for a small map.

quiz.q: For 5 cities, about how many distinct tours does brute force have to check?
options: 24, because it is 4 factorial
5, one tour starting from each city
120, because it is 5 factorial
10, because each pair of cities is counted once
quiz.why: The starting city is fixed, so the remaining 4 cities can be ordered in 4 factorial ways, which is 24 tours.

card.examTip: Write the recurrence for the (current city, visited set) state and the complexity 2^n - examiners usually give most marks for the state definition, not the numbers.

topics.title: Backtracking: General Method
topics.definition: Backtracking builds a solution one component at a time and abandons a partial solution as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer.

children.title: State space tree
children.definition: Every partial solution is a node of a tree; the root is the empty solution and the leaves are complete solutions or dead ends.

children.title: Promising and non-promising nodes
children.definition: A node is promising if it can still be completed into a valid solution; a non-promising node is pruned immediately.

children.title: Bounding functions
children.definition: A bound estimates the best value achievable under a node; if it cannot beat the current best, the whole subtree is skipped.

children.title: Control abstraction
children.definition: A recursive loop tries each candidate; if the partial solution is still promising, recurse, otherwise undo the choice and try the next.

children.title: Applications
children.definition: n-Queens, graph colouring, Hamiltonian cycle, sum of subsets, sudoku, maze solving and constraint satisfaction problems.

card.explanation: Backtracking is depth first search over the space of partial solutions, with early rejection of hopeless branches - that pruning is what makes it practical. At each step you extend the current partial solution with one more decision, and you stop expanding the moment the constraints are violated. If no decision works, you undo the last one and try another, which is literally 'backtracking'. The state space tree is still exponential in the worst case, but pruning usually makes the explored part far smaller than brute force.
card.example: Filling a sudoku: place a digit in a cell, and if it breaks a row or box rule, immediately erase it and try the next digit instead of finishing the whole grid wrongly.

quiz.q: A node in the state space tree is called promising when:
options: it can still lead to a valid solution
it is a leaf
its cost is lowest
it has children
quiz.why: Promising nodes are worth expanding; others are pruned.

quiz.q: Backtracking is essentially:
options: depth first search with pruning
dynamic programming
greedy selection
breadth first search
quiz.why: It dives deep into one choice and abandons it as soon as it becomes infeasible.

quiz.q: Which statement about backtracking is NOT correct?
options: It builds a solution one component at a time
A partial solution is abandoned as soon as it cannot work
It explores the state space tree breadth first
Its worst case is still exponential without pruning
quiz.why: Backtracking is depth first search over partial solutions; going breadth first would lose the undo-the-last-choice behaviour it relies on.

quiz.q: While filling a sudoku you place a digit that breaks a box rule. What does backtracking do next?
options: Starts the grid again from the first cell
Leaves the cell empty and moves on for good
Erases that digit and tries the next one
Fills the whole grid and fixes mistakes at the end
quiz.why: The violated constraint prunes that branch immediately, so the choice is undone and the next value is tried - the backtrack.

quiz.q: A state space tree has two choices at every step and a depth of 10. About how many nodes exist if nothing is pruned?
options: About 20, two choices per level
About 100, ten levels of ten branches
About 10, one node per level
About 1,000, since 2 raised to 10 is 1,024
quiz.why: Unpruned branching doubles at every level, so ten levels give roughly a thousand nodes, which is why pruning matters.

card.examTip: Draw the state space tree with promising nodes marked and pruned branches crossed out - the crossing out is what shows the technique, not the final answer.

topics.title: n-Queen Problem
topics.definition: The n-Queen problem places n queens on an n by n chessboard so that no two queens share a row, a column or a diagonal.

children.title: Constraints
children.definition: One queen per row and column, and no two queens on the same diagonal - which is checked by testing row plus column and row minus column values.

children.title: Solution as an n-tuple
children.definition: A solution is written as (x1, x2, ..., xn) where xi is the column of the queen placed in row i, so the row constraint is automatic.

children.title: Backtracking procedure
children.definition: Place a queen row by row, test each column for safety, recurse if safe, and remove the queen and try the next column if not.

children.title: 4-Queens example
children.definition: For n = 4 the solutions are (2, 4, 1, 3) and (3, 1, 4, 2), and the first placement (1, 3, ...) fails and is abandoned.

children.title: Number of solutions
children.definition: n = 1 gives 1 solution, n = 2 and n = 3 have none, and the count grows quickly from n = 4 onwards.

children.title: Complexity
children.definition: The plain search is factorial in the worst case, but pruning cuts it sharply; the time grows exponentially with n.

card.explanation: The chessboard rules make this a perfect backtracking problem: place queens one row at a time, and reject a column immediately if it is attacked. Because a queen attacks its entire row, column and both diagonals, you only need to check the columns and the two diagonals of the queens already placed. When a row has no safe column left, you undo the previous placement and continue from there - the classic backtrack. The solution is written as a tuple of column numbers, which is compact and lets the row constraint be satisfied for free.
card.example: Arranging four wedding photographers around a square hall so that no two stand in the same line of sight, front-to-back or diagonally.

quiz.q: A safe queen placement is tested by checking:
options: column and the two diagonals
only the diagonals
nothing, since rows differ
only the row
quiz.why: Rows are already distinct because one queen is placed per row, so columns and diagonals are checked.

quiz.q: How many solutions does the 4-Queens problem have?
quiz.why: The two solutions are (2,4,1,3) and (3,1,4,2).

quiz.q: Which statement about the n-Queen problem is NOT correct?
options: A solution is written by listing the row of each queen
When a row has no safe column, the previous row is undone
No two queens may share a row, a column or a diagonal
Queens are placed one row at a time during backtracking
quiz.why: A solution is written as a tuple of column numbers, one per row, which makes the row constraint free.

quiz.q: While placing queens you reach row 4 and find every column attacked. What does the algorithm do?
options: Places the queen in an attacked column anyway
Restarts the board from row 1 in a new order
Stops, because it has proved that no solution exists
Undoes the placement in row 3 and tries another column there
quiz.why: A dead end in one row means the previous choice was wrong, so it is undone and the next alternative is tried.

quiz.q: In the 4-Queens problem, one queen is placed in each row. How many ways are there to assign the columns before any diagonal check?
options: 256, because every square is chosen independently
24, because the four columns can be ordered in 4 factorial ways
4, because there are four rows to fill
16, because it is four rows of four squares
quiz.why: One queen per row means the four distinct columns can be permuted in 4 factorial = 24 ways, and the diagonal rules cut that down to 2.

card.examTip: Solve the 4-Queens case step by step, drawing the board at each stage and showing at least one pruned branch - that trace is the whole answer.

topics.title: Graph Colouring Problem
topics.definition: Graph colouring assigns colours to vertices so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour, using as few colours as possible.

children.title: Chromatic number
children.definition: The minimum number of colours needed to colour a graph properly, written as the chromatic number of the graph.

children.title: m-colourability
children.definition: The decision problem of whether a graph can be coloured with at most m colours.

children.title: Backtracking approach
children.definition: Assign colours to vertices one by one, reject a colour that matches a coloured neighbour, backtrack when no colour works for a vertex.

children.title: Bound on colours
children.definition: A graph can always be coloured with one more colour than its maximum degree, and by the four colour theorem every planar map needs at most four.

children.title: Applications
children.definition: Map colouring, exam timetable and register allocation in compilers, frequency assignment in mobile networks and seating conflict problems.

card.explanation: Colouring is really a conflict problem: vertices that must differ are joined by an edge, and the question is how few categories can separate them all. Backtracking works through the vertices in order, trying colours one at a time and rejecting a colour as soon as a neighbour already uses it. When a vertex has no valid colour, the algorithm backtracks to the previous vertex and changes its colour. The minimum number of colours, the chromatic number, is hard to compute in general, and deciding whether three colours suffice is itself an NP-complete problem.
card.example: Timetable scheduling: courses that share students must not be scheduled in the same time slot, so each time slot behaves like a colour.

quiz.q: The chromatic number of a graph is:
options: the minimum colours needed for a proper colouring
its maximum degree
the number of edges
its number of vertices
quiz.why: It is the smallest number of colours such that no adjacent pair shares a colour.

quiz.q: In graph colouring, backtracking is used to:
options: count edges
sort vertices
find a proper colouring by undoing bad colour choices
compute shortest paths
quiz.why: When a vertex cannot be coloured, the previous colour assignment is changed.

quiz.q: Which statement about graph colouring is NOT correct?
options: No two adjacent vertices may share a colour
The chromatic number is the minimum number of colours needed
Adjacent vertices may share a colour if they are far apart
Deciding whether three colours are enough is NP-complete
quiz.why: Sharing a colour is forbidden exactly when two vertices are adjacent, and distance on the page has nothing to do with it.

quiz.q: Courses that share students must not be held in the same slot. What does each time slot represent?
options: A vertex, with lecture halls as the edges
An edge weight, counting the shared students
The chromatic number of the timetable
A colour, with clashing courses as adjacent vertices
quiz.why: This is the card's own example: slots behave like colours and two courses that cannot clash are joined by an edge.

quiz.q: A graph joins every pair of its 5 vertices, so every pair is adjacent. How many colours does a proper colouring need?
options: 2, because every complete graph is bipartite
10, because there are ten edges to colour
5, because no two vertices may share a colour
1, because one colour covers all five vertices
quiz.why: In a complete graph every vertex touches every other, so each one needs its own colour and the chromatic number equals the vertex count.

card.examTip: Explain with the map colouring example, then show the backtracking tree for a small graph - state the chromatic number at the end.

topics.title: Complexity Classes: P and NP
topics.definition: P is the class of decision problems solvable in polynomial time, and NP is the class of problems whose proposed solutions can be verified in polynomial time.

children.title: Decision problem
children.definition: A problem whose answer is yes or no, such as 'is there a tour shorter than 500 km?' - the standard form used in complexity theory.

children.title: Class P
children.definition: Problems solvable by a deterministic algorithm in time O(n^k), such as sorting, searching and shortest paths.

children.title: Class NP
children.definition: Problems for which a given solution can be checked quickly, even if finding it is hard; every P problem is also in NP.

children.title: The P versus NP question
children.definition: Whether every problem whose solution can be verified quickly can also be solved quickly; it is open, and most researchers believe P is not equal to NP.

children.title: Non-deterministic view
children.definition: NP can be described as problems that a non-deterministic machine guesses and verifies in polynomial time, which is equivalent to the certificate view.

card.explanation: Complexity classes group problems by how their difficulty grows with input size, which lets us say something useful even when an exact algorithm is unknown. P contains the problems we can definitely solve quickly: sorting a list, finding a shortest path, checking whether a number is prime. NP is broader: it allows problems where recognising a correct answer is easy even if discovering it is not, such as checking whether a given tour is shorter than 500 km. Since verifying can never be harder than solving, P is contained in NP, and whether the two are actually equal is the most famous open question in computer science.
card.example: Solving a jigsaw is tedious, but seeing a finished jigsaw and confirming it is correct takes seconds - that gap is exactly the difference between solving and verifying.

quiz.q: Class P contains problems that:
options: can be solved in polynomial time
have no solution
need exponential space
can only be verified quickly
quiz.why: P is the set of decision problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic algorithm.

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
options: P equals NP
P is a subset of NP
NP is a subset of P
P and NP are disjoint
quiz.why: Anything solvable quickly can also be verified quickly, so P is contained in NP.

quiz.q: Which statement about the classes P and NP is NOT correct?
options: Verifying a solution is never harder than finding one
P contains the problems solvable in polynomial time
NP allows easy verification even when solving is hard
P is known to be a strictly smaller class than NP
quiz.why: Whether P equals NP is still open; all we know for certain is that P is contained in NP.

quiz.q: A classmate hands you a finished jigsaw and you can see at once that it fits together. What does that show about NP?
options: Checking an answer can be easy even if finding it was hard
Solving must be just as easy as checking
The problem cannot be solved by any algorithm
The problem is in P but not in NP
quiz.why: This is the card's own picture of NP: verification is cheap even when the search that produced the answer was expensive.

quiz.q: Sorting n numbers with a good algorithm costs n log n comparisons. Which class does that place sorting in?
options: NP-complete, because everything reduces to it
P, because n log n is polynomial time
NP-hard, because sorting uses comparisons
Neither P nor NP, because it is a sorting task
quiz.why: Polynomial time solvability is the definition of P, and n log n grows more slowly than n squared.

card.examTip: Define decision problem first, then P, then NP, and finish with the containment P within NP - that is the standard five-mark structure.

topics.title: NP-Hard and NP-Complete Problems
topics.definition: A problem is NP-hard if every NP problem reduces to it, and NP-complete if it is NP-hard and also belongs to NP.

children.title: Polynomial time reduction
children.definition: Problem A reduces to B if any instance of A can be rewritten as an instance of B in polynomial time, so a solver for B also solves A.

children.title: NP-hard
children.definition: A problem is NP-hard when every problem in NP reduces to it; an NP-hard problem need not itself be in NP, and it may be undecidable.

children.title: NP-complete
children.definition: A problem that is both in NP and NP-hard - the hardest problems in NP, such as satisfiability, clique, vertex cover and Hamiltonian cycle.

children.title: Cook's theorem
children.definition: The satisfiability problem (SAT) was the first problem proved NP-complete, which is why it anchors all further proofs.

children.title: Dealing with NP-complete problems
children.definition: Use approximation algorithms, heuristics, branch and bound, or solve restricted special cases in polynomial time.

card.explanation: Once one hard problem is identified, others can be proved hard by translating them into it, which is the idea of reduction. A problem is NP-hard if every NP problem can be transformed into it, meaning an efficient solution would immediately solve all of NP; if it is also in NP itself, it is called NP-complete. Satisfiability is the anchor example from Cook's theorem, and clique, vertex cover, graph colouring, Hamiltonian cycle and TSP follow from it. In practice, NP-complete problems are attacked with approximation, heuristics or branch and bound rather than exact exponential search.
card.example: Timetable clashes, delivery routing and exam scheduling in a college are all NP-complete in general, so colleges use heuristics that give good, not provably optimal, schedules.

quiz.q: A problem is NP-complete if it is:
options: in NP only
NP-hard and in NP
solvable in polynomial time
NP-hard only
quiz.why: NP-completeness requires both membership in NP and NP-hardness.

quiz.q: Which problem was the first proved NP-complete?
options: Graph colouring
Clique
Travelling salesman
Satisfiability (SAT)
quiz.why: Cook's theorem established SAT as the first NP-complete problem.

quiz.q: Which statement about NP-hard and NP-complete problems is NOT correct?
options: A problem in NP that is NP-hard is NP-complete
An NP-hard problem must itself belong to NP
Reduction is the tool used to prove other problems hard
Every NP problem reduces to an NP-hard problem
quiz.why: NP-hard problems need not be in NP at all; only when they are also in NP do they earn the name NP-complete.

quiz.q: A college must build a clash-free timetable. Why do colleges use heuristics instead of an exact answer?
options: Heuristics always return the optimal timetable
The problem is NP-complete, so a good schedule is used
The problem is in P, so heuristics are merely faster
Timetables have no constraints left to check
quiz.why: Timetabling is NP-complete, so colleges settle for schedules that are good rather than provably optimal.

quiz.q: An NP-complete problem is reduced to a new problem in polynomial time. What does that prove about the new problem?
options: It is NP-hard, because every NP problem reduces to it
It is in P, because the reduction itself runs quickly
It has no solution under any circumstances
It is easier than the problem it came from
quiz.why: A reduction from a known hard problem carries the hardness across, so the new problem is NP-hard and NP-complete if it is also in NP.

card.examTip: Define reduction, then NP-hard, then NP-complete, and note that NP-complete means 'NP-hard and in NP' - missing that last clause is the most common mistake.
